The meaning is as follows: if, even when there is a contradiction with grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*)—as in "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke, like a kitchen" (*parvato vahnimān, dhūmāt, mahānasavat*), or "there is no jar on the ground" (*na ghaṭo bhūtale*) versus the cognition "there is a jar on the ground" (*ghaṭo bhūtale*) and so forth—if both grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and the resulting comprehension of the sentence meaning (*anvayabodha*) are accepted, then one should also abandon the postulation of the *spṛhī* suffix for the dative case. The underlying intention is that, since the equality regarding compliance with grammatical rules is established, it is improper to apply the "half-old woman" logic (*ardhajaratīya*). || 18 ||

He states that suffixes such as *ini* prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and other kārakas connect only with the action: "Just as [the abstract noun] 'going' and others, which lack a physical form, connect with objects such as a village..."
In the same way, the action remains connected in such cases as "having previously done" (kṛtapūrvī) and so forth.

That which has no separate apprehension—that is, no distinct grasping—is "without a separate grasp" (*avigrahā*), meaning it has become subordinate (*guṇībhūtā*). Just as in the expression "he went to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), the action, although subordinate as the meaning of the *kta* suffix, is connected with the objects such as the village; likewise, in the expression "one who previously made a mat" (*kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*), the meaning is that [the action] is subordinate to the verbal roots such as *kṛ*.

Nor should it be argued that since the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) will be explained as residing in the verbal root alone (*vṛtti-mātra*), and since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is included therein as a part of the word-meaning, how can there be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with it? For in cases of constant dependence (*nitya-sāpekṣa*), a connection is accepted even with a single constituent part, as in "Devadatta’s teacher’s house" (*devadattasya gurukulam*) and "Caitra’s grandson" (*caitrasya naptā*). The same should be understood in cases such as "cooking for the sake of eating" (*bhoktuṃ pākaḥ*) and "cooking after having eaten" (*bhuktvā pākaḥ*). || 19 ||
Having raised the suspicion of over-extension regarding the meanings of the *kṛtvas* suffixes, he provides the resolution;

suspecting an over-extension, he resolves it: "If it be argued that the meanings of *kṛtvas* would apply to the *ktavatu*, *tumun*, and *vans* suffixes as well, [we reply] they do indeed exist in certain cases."
An over-extension (atiprasaṅga) should not be raised, because it relies upon the actual expression [of the word]. || 20 ||

In examples such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking for the purpose of eating") and *bhuktavā pākaḥ* ("cooking after having eaten"), [the rule] applies: "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when one action is for the sake of another action" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.3.10).

Just as the suffixes *tumun* and others—though prescribed for actions occurring at earlier and later times when there is a word denoting an action (*kriyāvācaka*) as a subordinate element (*upapada*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.21, *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*—arise by taking that [action] as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), so too should the suffixes expressing the sense of *kṛtvas* (times/occurrences) arise. For instance, in the case of *ekaḥ pākaḥ* ("one cooking"), [the suffix *sac* would apply]; in *dvau pākau*, *trayaḥ*, and *catvāraḥ* ("two, three, or four cookings"), [the suffix *suc* would apply] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.18, *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc*; and in the case of *pañca* ("five [cookings]"), the suffix *kṛtvasuc* would apply.

If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of expressions such as "cooking once," "two, three, or four times cooking," and so on, [the author replies] that this is an accepted consequence (iṣṭāpatti), because we observe forms such as "dvirvacanam" (reduplication).

He states "atiprasaṅga... to indicate that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) due to non-usage (anabhidhāna); the sense is that the matter should be resolved according to the statement of the learned authorities (abhiyukta): "The root *vac* is not employed with the suffix *anti*. Some, however, maintain that in the rule "saṅkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane," the inclusion of the word *kriyā* (action) is redundant, since its meaning is obtained by implication (*sāmarthya*) through the possibility of repetition belonging to that very action.

And thus, in order to obtain a meaning that consists solely of the action to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the word *tat* (it) must be stated; and since such [an action] is not present in cases like *pākaḥ* (cooking), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, regarding the term *dvirvacana* (reduplication), it should be explained either by the etymology "the use of a word twice is reduplication" (*dviḥprayogo dvirvacanam*), or by relying on the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59). So they say. || 20 ||

To address the doubt—namely, "In the Siddhānta, since expressive power (*śakti*) consists in the capacity to convey meaning, and since understanding occurs for those who have grasped the power of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it is necessary [that this power resides there]; therefore, how is it determined that *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone and not by the suffix?"—the author provides the following resolution:
"It is based on the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the relationship between the qualified (*bhedya*) and the qualifier (*bhedaka*)."
Even in the absence of that [external object], correctness is established; here, the cognition itself is not denied. || 21 ||

The "differentiable" (*bhedyam*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and the "differentiator" (*bhedakam*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); the correctness (*sādhutvam*) [of a word] is based on the distinction between their relationship. This is the meaning: the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is intent upon the correctness of words. For the Mīmāṃsakas—who assert that the status of being a power (*śaktitvam*) belongs to the property postulated as the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*) within that very [correctness]—the status of being a power and correctness are one and the same. Thus, according to their method, it is said that the determination of power is identical to the determination of correctness.

Even under the theory of residual potency (*atiriktaśaktivāda*), the verbal suffixes would indeed be grammatically incorrect (*asādhutā*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). And thus, just as there is the use of the instrumental case where the dative is required, so too would there be the use of the verbal suffix for the productive activity denoted by the root-meaning; consequently, due to the employment of an incorrect word in a ritual act (*yājña-karma*), those who possess the linguistic training of other systems (i.e., non-Mīmāṃsakas) would certainly incur the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) resulting from the transgression of the prohibition "one should not speak untruth."

Objection: In your view, the prohibition "one shall not speak untruth" would not be established as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); since the agent is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it would—by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*)—be for the sake of the person alone (*puruṣārtha*). For its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice arises from context (*prakaraṇa*), and that is sublated when there is a conflict with direct statement. Reply: This is not so, because this has already been refuted by the principle that "the meaning of the verbal suffix is a qualifier. Indeed, the agent, being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), is not capable of taking the prohibition as its own auxiliary (*aṅga*).

However, since meditation (bhāvanā) is capable of grasping that [object] as its primary focus, by virtue of the context, it pertains solely to the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha). Or, let it be a duty for the person associated with the sacrifice (kratuyuktapuruṣadharma), because there is no difference in its performance. This has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa*, citing the injunction regarding the mantra stated in the passage: "One who is yawning should recite: 'In me, may skill and resolve [dwell]'."

[Objection: But surely, if the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), then no understanding of it could arise from it, because the knowledge of correctness (*sādhutvajñāna*) is a cause for verbal comprehension. To this he says: "Comprehension" (*bodha*). Let there indeed be comprehension even in the case of incorrectness due to an error regarding correctness, just as in the case of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). However, the incorrectness itself would certainly remain; this is the sense. In reality, the knowledge of correctness is not a [necessary] cause, nor is the ascertainment of its absence an obstacle; we shall explain this under the verse beginning with "The incorrect [is understood] by inference" (*asādhuranumānena*). || 21 ||
In this *Bhūṣaṇasāra* composed by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, the son of Raṅgoji Bhaṭṭa, the determination of the meaning of verbal roots and finite verbs is complete. (1)
Thus ends the first section, the examination of the meaning of verbal roots and the general meaning of finite verbs, in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra composed by the illustrious Koṇḍabhaṭṭa.
The Determination of the Meaning of the Tense Markers (Lakāras). Now begins the determination of the meaning of the tense markers.

The commentary on the *ṭi* suffixes explains the meaning of each of the ten verbal suffixes (*lakāra*): [they are used] for the present, the unperceived (past), the future, and that which will come to be tomorrow.
The *laṭ* and other [tenses and moods] should be understood as occurring respectively in the case of injunctions and so forth, as well as in requests and so forth. || 22 ||
The six suffixes beginning with *laṭ* are to be understood as corresponding to these six meanings in their respective order.
**The Definition of the Meaning of *Laṭ***:

Thus, *laṭ* is used for the present tense, according to the rule "In the sense of the present, *laṭ*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.123). Presentness consists either in being commenced but not yet completed, or in being distinct from the past and the future. In expressions such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), since that [present action] exists in the interval between the acts of placing the pot on the fire and taking it off, the use of *laṭ* occurs.
Regarding the determination of the present tense in expressions such as "the self exists" (*ātmā asti*):

in cases like "the self exists" (*ātmā asti*) or "the mountains exist" (*parvatāḥ santi*), since the actions of various kings belonging to those respective times are impermanent, the state of being present must be inferred by taking into account the origination and so forth of that which is qualified by those [actions]. For it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In this world, the actions of past, future, and present kings constitute the domain of the verb 'to stand' (*astiṣṭhateḥ*). Furthermore:
"Everything else changes, but the Self does not waver."
Therefore, the existence of mountains and the like is differentiated by means of another form.

Thus it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*. In this same manner, Vedic passages such as "Darkness was," "That which was covered by the void," and "I alone existed first, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future," are also to be applied.

Whether the state of being present (*vartamānatva*) is indicated (*dyotyatva*) or directly expressed (*vācyatva*), that state of being present and so forth is indicated by the suffixes *laṭ* and others; for when the general action denoted by the root is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as qualified by that [temporal state], the *laṭ* and other suffixes serve to convey the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that form [of the temporal state] is indeed directly expressed (*vācya*) by the *laṭ* and other suffixes. Otherwise, the suffixes...
Another alternative view is that it would result in the loss of [the verb's] denotative capacity (*vācakatva*).

Regarding the meaning of the *liṭ* suffix, he states "in the case of the remote past" (*parokṣe*), based on the rule "the *liṭ* suffix is used for the remote past" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.115). Time is first of all twofold, distinguished as "contemporary" (*adyatana*) and "non-contemporary" (*anadyatana*). Each of these two types is further divided into the forms of the past and the future. Among these, the meaning is that the *liṭ* suffix is used for the past that is non-contemporary and remote. Consequently, there is no use of the *liṭ* suffix for what is contemporary and past, for what is non-contemporary and future, or even for what is past but not remote. Furthermore, "remoteness" (*parokṣatva*) consists in not being the object of a cognition characterized by such a cognitive state (*viṣayatā*) as "I perceive [it] directly."
Regarding the phrase "in the absence [of perception]," there is a doubt that it serves no purpose as an exclusion, and its refutation follows:

One should not suspect that the term "in the absence [of perception]" (*parokṣe*) is redundant because action is beyond the senses—based on the *Bhāṣya* statement, "This thing called action is entirely imperceptible, consisting of successive parts, and cannot be shown as a solidified whole. Even if it is impossible to demonstrate it as a solidified whole, it is possible for it to be the object of the cognition "I perceive" part by part. Otherwise, in the case of the expression "Look, the deer runs," action could not function as the object of seeing. This is how it appears.

In this context, what is intended by "remoteness" (*pārokṣya*) is precisely the remoteness of those means conducive to an action that are already engaged in activity; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Some also state "of those engaged in activity" (*vyāpārāviṣṭānām*) in order to conform with examples such as "this one cooked" (*ayaṃ papāca*).
[This addresses] the doubt regarding the absence of self-remoteness in respect to one's own action, and its resolution.

If it is argued that the statement, “Udayana spread forth the *Kiraṇāvalī*,” is possible because one’s own action is perceptible to oneself, this is entirely inconsistent. For even if it were established that one’s own activity is imperceptible due to distraction (*vyāsaṅga*) and so forth, the *liṭ* suffix could not occur in that context; since the composition of a treatise—consisting of the arrangement of words that produces a determination of the meaning of a scripture achievable through intense mental concentration—is an action of spreading that is neither recent nor past, the conditions for the *anadyatana* (not of today) and *atīta* (past) [required by *liṭ*] are absent. Therefore, the meaning must be the *luṅ* (aorist).

He states the meaning of *luṭ*: "occurring tomorrow" (*śvo bhāvinī*). This means occurring at a time other than the current day, based on the rule "The suffix *luṭ* is used for what is to occur in the non-current day" (*anadyatane luṭ*, Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.15). For example, as in "it will happen tomorrow" (*śvo bhavitā*). He states the meaning of *lṛṭ*: "will be" (*bhaviṣyati*). This means in general future time, based on the rule "The suffix *lṛṭ* is used for the remainder [i.e., the future]" (*lṛṭ śeṣe ca*, Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.13). For example, as in "the pot will be" (*ghaṭo bhaviṣyati*). And its essential nature (*tattva*) is: having an origination at a time that is the counter-positive of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the present.

He states the meaning of *leṭ*: "in the sense of *liṅ* and so forth," based on the rule *liṅarthe leṭ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.7). It will be stated that the meaning of *liṅ* consists of injunction (*vidhi*) and the like.

He states the meaning of *loṭ*: "supplication (*prārthanā*) and so forth. By the phrase "and so forth," injunction and benediction (*āśis*) are included, as this is understood from the two rules *āśiṣi liṅloṭau* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.173) and *loṭ ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.162), as in examples such as "May there be the grace of Śiva for you. The meaning of these two is indeed the same as the meaning of *liṅ*, because all three share an identical meaning; thus, their determination is achieved simply by determining that [meaning of *liṅ*]. || 22 ||
Regarding the meaning of *laṅ* and the others:
he states the meaning of those [suffixes] marked with *ṅ* in their respective order beginning with *laṅ*:
"The suffixes *laṅ* and so forth [are used] for what occurred yesterday, for instigation and the like, and for simple past time."
And when there is the non-occurrence of an action, the conditional suffix (lṛṅ) is prescribed for both the past and the future.

The meaning of *laṅ*: he states the meaning of *laṅ* as "past non-today" (*hyo bhūta*). This means "past not belonging to the current day," based on the rule: "The suffix *laṅ* is used for the past not of today" (*anadyatane laṅ*, Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.111). For example: "His son was born" (*asya putro 'bhavat*), and so forth.
The meaning of *liṅ*.

He states the meaning of the *liṅ* suffix: "in instigation (*preraṇā*) and so forth," based on the rule: "The *liṅ* [is used] in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), permission (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*sampraśna*), and supplication (*prārthana*)" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.161). Among these, *vidhi* is instigation; it is the impelling of a subordinate person, such as a servant. *Nimantraṇa* is the performance of a duty; the meaning is the impelling of a daughter's son and others toward an obligatory act, such as a funeral feast (*śrāddha*). *Āmantraṇa* is permission to act according to one's own will. *Adhīṣṭa* is an activity preceded by honor. *Sampraśna* is deliberation.
Alternatively, expressibility [of the meaning] consists in its being an instigation (pravarttanā) accompanied by these four [factors], because of parsimony (lāghava). And it has been said:
"The nature of instigation is woven through all four [of these];
the optative suffix (liṅ) should be applied to that alone—what is the use of intending to express the distinctions?"
"Whether for the purpose of explaining the logical system (nyāya), or else for the sake of elaboration,
the fourfold beginning with 'vidhi' was established at the outset.

Furthermore, the state of being an instigator (*pravartanātva*) consists in being the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the objecthood (*viṣayatā*) of the cognition that generates activity (*pravṛtti*).
Since that [property]— the state of being a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatva)— exists [in the sacrifice], that alone is the meaning of the injunctive suffix (vidhi).

Although this [exclusion] applies to the status of being achievable by effort (kṛtisādhyatva) and so forth as well— since even the knowledge of that [achievable-by-effort-ness] is a motivator— nevertheless, because that [achievable-by-effort-ness] is obtained in all cases such as sacrifices through worldly convention itself, it cannot be the meaning [of the suffix] due to being obtainable from another source (anyalabhyatva).

Furthermore, the knowledge that an action is not followed by a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñāna*) is not the cause [of activity], because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) through the absence of aversion (*dveṣābhāva*). Moreover, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since even for a lustful person who believes an act leads to hell, activity occurs when there is an intense desire and an absence of aversion. Therefore, being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) alone is the instigation (*pravarttanā*).
And as Mandana Miśra has said:
"For men, there is no other motivator toward actions than their being a means to a desired end."
"They declare that dharma is the cause of engagement and that [the suffix] *pravartanā* is the instigation. This has been explained in detail in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those meanings such as the relation of cause and effect mentioned in the rules "The optative (*liṅ*) is used for cause and effect" (Pāṇini 3.3.156) and "The optative (*liṅ*) and imperative (*loṭ*) are used in the sense of benediction" (Pāṇini 3.3.173) are included. For example: "Whoever should strike a Brāhmaṇa, him one should punish with a hundred [fines]."

The meaning of the *luṅ* [suffix]. He states the meaning of *luṅ*: "in the mere past" (*bhūtamātre*), which means "in the general past. This is because of the rule: "The *luṅ* [suffix is used] when the past is intended" (*bhūte*, governing "the *luṅ* suffix," Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.110). Here, "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) is defined as "being the counter-positive of a currently existing destruction" (*vidyamānadhvaṃsapratiyogitva*). Since this [definition] applies without obstruction to an action (*kriyā*), the expression "the jar existed" (*ghaṭo 'bhūt*) is used even when the jar is present. The cognition [resulting from this] is: "An activity conducive to origination, etc., which has as its locus something non-different from the jar, is the counter-positive of a currently existing destruction. [This is] the division of time.

Here is the summary: Time is twofold—present (*adyatana*) and non-present (*anadyatana*). The former is threefold, distinguished as past, future, and present. The latter is twofold—past and future. Among these, the *laṭ* [present tense] is used for the state of being present. The *luṅ* [aorist] is used for mere pastness. The *lṛṭ* [future tense] is used for mere futurity. When there is a desire to express an additional meaning such as the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), the *lṛṅ* [conditional] is used for both [past and future]. When the non-present is intended to be expressed as past, the *laṅ* [imperfect] is used. In that same context, when the intention is to express remoteness from the speaker's perception (*parokṣatva*), the *liṭ* [perfect] is used. For a similar future time, the *luṭ* [periphrastic future] is used; thus it should be understood. This is the meaning of the *lṛṅ*.

He states the meaning of *lṛṅ*: "When there is..."—the sense is that *lṛṅ* occurs when there is a non-occurrence (*atipatti*), i.e., a non-accomplishment, of an action, which is understood to have been in the past or is yet to be in the future, provided there exists a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) between them. This is based on the rule: "The conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used when there is a cause for the [conditional] *liṅ*, provided there is a non-occurrence of the action" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.138). The "cause for *liṅ*" refers to the causal relationship and so forth. For example: "If there had been good rain, there would have been an abundant harvest"; "If fire had blazed up, he would have cooked the rice," and so on.

In this context, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "The absence of an activity conducive to burning, which has as its locus something non-different from fire, is caused by the absence of an activity conducive to softening (*viklitti*), which has as its locus something non-different from boiled rice. It should be understood in this manner.

And this explanation of the meaning is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), since we observe that [the suffix] is prescribed in many other meanings as well. It has been stated according to the view of another school that its expressive power (*śakti*) resides in these very meanings because they are well-known, while in other cases there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the sequence of these [suffixes] is determined by the sequence of their phonetic appendages (*anubandha*). For this very reason, the *leṭ* is designated as "the fifth *l*-suffix" (*pañcamo lakāraḥ*) by the Mīmāṃsakas; such is the direction of the argument. || 23 ||
Thus ends the second section, the determination of the specific meanings of the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*), in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*.
Now, the determination of the meanings of case-endings (*sub*).
He states the meaning of the case-endings: "The locus (*āśraya*), the limit (*avadhi*), the intended object (*uddeśya*), the relation (*sambandha*), or indeed power (*śakti*)."
The meanings of the case endings (*sup*) are distributed according to their respective functions, as stated in the Bhāṣya: "the object (*karman*) and so forth. (24)

The meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the locus (*āśraya*); the meaning of the second, third, and seventh cases is the locus. For instance: "The second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.2). And that [object] is "that which is most desired by the agent"—meaning the locus of the result produced by the action; for it is precisely because the object possesses the result produced by the action that it is what is most desired by the agent. This is also appropriate because it includes [the rule] "and likewise that which is not desired but is connected in the same way" (*tathāyuktañcānīpsitam*, Pāṇini 1.4.50). Since the states of being desired or undesired do not appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), their utility lies only in the technical designation (*saṃjñā*); they do not enter into the category of the expressed meaning (*vācyakoṭi*).
And the state of being a locus (*āśrayatva*) is a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) in the form of an indivisible power (*akhaṇḍa-śakti*).

Thus, since the action and the result are already obtained by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, the meaning [of the accusative] is exclusively the locus, which is not obtainable through any other means. And its essence is a delimitor in the form of an indivisible power. In the case of "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), there is the status of object (*karmmatā*) because of being the locus of the softening (*viklitti*).
Even for verbs such as *jñā* ("to know") and others, there is indeed a primary transitivity (*sakarmakatva*).

In the case of "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), [the pot is the locus] because it is the locus of origination, and because origination is the meaning of the verbal root. In the case of "he knows" (*jānāti*), [the object is the locus] because it is the locus of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning, which consists in the removal of an obscuration. This is necessary even in cases involving past, future, or otherwise non-perceptible objects; otherwise, the undesirable consequence would arise that one could say, "I do not know it as before. Furthermore, the status of the past and so forth as loci—and their being loci by way of being objects—is established either through the Nyāya view of the locus of knowledge, or through the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). And it has been said:
"When the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of entities is admitted, that itself is their non-existence.

Once concealment has attained its sequence, it is perceived as 'perishing'. This is the objection regarding the possibility of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*) receiving the designation of "object" (*karman*), and its resolution.

Now, one might object: in the sentence "Caitra goes to the village," since Caitra, like the village, is the locus of the result produced by the action—namely, the conjunction with the village—he would incur the status of an *object* (*karman*), leading to the undesirable consequence that one could say "Caitra goes to Caitra. Furthermore, when Caitra goes from Prayāga to Kāśī, there would be the undesirable consequence of saying "He goes to Prayāga," because the conjunction produced by the action exists in Kāśī, and the disjunction [produced by the action] also exists in Prayāga. If this is argued, we reply: no, for even though Caitra, like the village, is indeed the locus of the result, [the definition of an object does not apply here].

Because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "agent" (*kartṛ*) subverts the designation of "object" (*karman*), the usage *caitraścaitram* ("Caitra [acts upon] Caitra") is impossible; for in the production of the accusative case, the technical designation itself is the regulating factor. Otherwise, just as in the case of *gamayati kṛṣṇaṃ gokulam* ("He causes Kṛṣṇa to go to Gokula"), the same would apply here, and the word *kṛṣṇa* in *pācayati kṛṣṇena* ("He causes Kṛṣṇa to cook") would also result in taking the accusative case.

If it is argued that there would be a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) such as "Caitra [is] Caitra" in this case, we say no; for we accept such a result for those who have acquired proficiency (vyutpanna) in that manner. Alternatively, let another causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) be stated: "The presentation of a substratum (āśraya) that is not the locus of the action (vyāpāra) denoted by the verbal root is the cause of a cognition whose qualificandum (viśeṣya) is the fruit (phala) denoted by the verbal root, related through the relation of being a mode (prakāratā). In the present instance, there is no fault, because Caitra is not non-locus of the action.

Furthermore, although it might be conceivable that Prayāga possesses the status of an object (*karma*), this is not the case; for it has already been stated that by the phrase "produced by the action" (*kriyājanya*), what is intended is precisely the possession of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning as co-occurrent with that action.
Herein lies the view of the Naiyāyikas.

The Naiyāyikas, however, in order to avoid the first fault, take "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) as a qualifier for the result, and in order to avoid the second fault, they maintain that "being the delimitor of the root-meaning" (*dhātvarthatā'vacchedakatva*) is also expressed by the accusative case-ending. This "residing in another" connects with the action denoted by the verbal root, precisely because a distinct causal relation must be postulated in this manner. Furthermore, "otherness" (*paratva*) is understood through the accusative as being relative to the meaning of its own stem (the agent).

Thus, in such cases as "Caitra cooks the rice," [the rice is the object] because it possesses the softening (*viklitti*)—which is the delimitor of the root-meaning—produced by an operation residing in something other than the rice itself.

"The state of being the object (*karmatā*) belongs to the rice. As for the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), they say it is: 'Caitra possesses an effort that generates an action inherent in something other than the rice, which is conducive to the softening (*viklitti*)—the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root—inherent in the rice. This is the refutation of the Naiyāyika position.

We do not accept that [position], because properties such as "residing in another" (parasamavetatva) are not denotable due to their complexity (gaurava). Is the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding the accusative case (dvitīyā) or regarding verbal cognition (śābdabodha)? Not the first, because even if those [properties] were stated as denotable, the problem would remain as it was; for just as in "gamayati kṛṣṇaṃ gokulam," there would result the occurrence of the accusative in "pācayati kṛṣṇaṃ gopaḥ," and just as in "taṇḍulaṃ pacati caitraḥ," there would result the occurrence of "taṇḍulaṃ pacyate svayameva."

Because it is the substratum of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which consists of contact with fire inhering in something other than the rice grains conducive to softening (*viklitti*). The over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding verbal cognition is also refuted by the aforementioned method; for even if "inherence in another" (*parasamavetatva*) were the denotation (*śakyatva*), there would be further complexity due to having to postulate numerous causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) to secure the desired syntactic connection (*iṣṭānvaya*) between "anotherness" (*paratva*) and "inherence in another"—as is clear in the *Bhūṣaṇa*.
This sevenfold division of action (*karman*) is as follows:
This is of seven kinds:—

It is considered threefold—as that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*)—and that [object] which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) is the *karma*; another fourfold classification has also been devised.
That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent,
that which is not designated by other names, and that which has another as its antecedent.
Thus, from the *Vākyapadīya*:
"That which is non-existent [before] and is produced, or that which exists and is manifested by birth—that is the *nirvartya* (produced) object;
but the *vikārya* (modified) object is established as being of two kinds."
Some [transformation] arises from the destruction of the original nature, like the ashes of wood and the like;
some arises through the production of a different quality, like the modification of gold and the like.

When the accomplishment of those things whose specific modifications have been produced by action cannot be apprehended either through perception or through inference, that is said to be "attainable" (prāpya).

And it is stated in that very same [work]: "He makes a pot" and so forth is the first [type]. "He makes wood into ash" and "He makes gold into an earring" are the second. "He sees a pot" is the third. "He touches grass" is the indifferent (*udāsīna*). "He eats poison" is the hateful (*dveṣya*). "He milks a cow" is expressed by another designation (*saṃjñāntara*).
"He becomes enraged at a cruel person" is preceded by another [agent] (*anyapūrva*).

The third [case] is the agentive third case; its meaning is the locus of the agentive third case. For it is said: "The independent is the agent" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.54), and independence consists in being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal root.

"Agenthood is always intended for that *kāraka* whose action is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*)," according to the *Vākyapadīya*. For this very reason, such expressions as "the pot cooks," "the fire cooks," "the fuel pieces cook," and "the rice cooks by itself" are logically consistent, based on the principle: "When the action belonging to a particular entity is denoted by the verbal root, then that entity is the agent."

Regarding the demonstration that it is illogical for a single entity to possess two designations at once: one might object—how can this be reconciled with the determination made by the venerable Vyāsa in the Sūtra *Brahma-sūtra* 1.2.4, "And because of the designation of [it] as both object and agent," concerning the statement "consisting of mind, having the vital breath as its body"? If the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) were the individual soul (*jīva*), then the subsequent designation in the remainder of the passage—"Thus, having departed from here, I shall attain him"—which describes it as both the object of attainment and the agent, would be contradictory. It is replied: If the individual soul itself were the object of knowledge, then it would have to be designated as both the object of attainment and the agent. [However, in the present case, these two designations belong to different entities.]

It has been stated by means of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to possess two designations at once, because the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) would sublate the designation of object (*karman-saṃjñā*). Consequently, the accusative case in "etam" would not occur. Moreover, in the case of a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛtā*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the application of the *yaṅ* suffix and so forth. Thus, through the medium of a contradiction in linguistic expression, this becomes the cause of the distinction [between the two]. And so, since the aspect of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is obtainable from the verbal root, the meaning of the instrumental case is merely the substratum (*āśraya*). This concludes the refutation of the Naiyāyika definition of the agent.

The status of being the instigator of the circle of causal factors (*kārakacakraprayoktṛtva*) and the status of being the substratum of the action (*kṛtyāśrayatva*) are under-defined (*avyāpta*) in the case of "the staff acts" (*daṇḍaḥ karoti*). This agent (*kartṛ*) is threefold: the pure (*śuddha*), the instigating cause (*prayojako hetuḥ*), and the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: in "Hari is served by me" (*mayā hariḥ sevyate*), [the meaning is] an operation conducive to the service having Hari as its object, whose substratum is non-different from me; in "it is caused to be produced by Hari" (*kāryyate hariṇā*), [the meaning is] an operation conducive to production, whose substratum is non-different from Hari; and in "he causes Kṛṣṇa to go to Gokula" (*gamayati kṛṣṇaṃ gokulam*), [the meaning is] an operation conducive to such an operation (of going) which has Kṛṣṇa as its substratum and is conducive to going having Gokula as its object.
The meaning of the instrumental case [ending] is instrumentality (*karaṇa*).

Furthermore, the denotata of the instrumental case are both the locus (*āśraya*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). For instance: "The most effective cause is the instrument" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.42). The sense of the suffix *tamap* is excellence (*prakarṣa*). And that [excellence] consists in possessing an operation that produces the result without any intervention.
This is the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
And a cause is that which possesses such an operation. As it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"When, in a particular instance, the accomplishment of an action is intended to follow immediately after the operation of something, that thing is then designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*)."
In reality, that [agenthood] is indefinable, for no entity is established as such; since we observe the intended expression, "the food is cooked by the pot. Thus it is said.

By the phrase "is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣyate*), [the author] indicates that since multiple [grammatical relations] cannot occur simultaneously, there is scope for the second and seventh case endings (*dvitīyā-saptamī*) and so forth.
The statement "the agent is the subject matter of the treatise" (*kartā śāstrārtha*) serves as a rebuttal to the contradiction with the *adhikaraṇa* (section) of the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā*.

Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the objection raised in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* section (*Brahmasūtra* 2.3.33)—specifically in the sūtra "Because of the reversal of capacity" (*śaktiviparyayāt*), which states that if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were the agent, a reversal of its instrumental capacity would result—would be untenable. This is because the intended meaning is that one would be postulating a reversal of capacity without any basis for doing so, by ascribing agency to that very thing which has been established by another scriptural passage (*Śruti*) as an instrument, namely: "Having taken back the consciousness of these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) through his own consciousness. (Brhadaranyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17).

In reality, however, this is merely an additional argument, as has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa*, starting with the observation that it is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* itself under the section [sūtra] 2.3.40, "And as the carpenter, in both ways."

The meaning of the locative case is also the locus (*āśraya*). According to the rule *saptamyadhikaraṇe ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.36), the locative case is used for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). And that [locus] is the "substratum" (*ādhāra*) according to the rule *ādhāro'dhikaraṇam* (Pāṇini 1.4.45). Its essence is the state of being a locus (*āśrayatva*). In this context, the aspect of being a locus is the primary denotation (*śakya*), while its essence is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Now, would not the technical designation "locus" apply to the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the instrument (*karaṇa*) merely by virtue of their being loci? It would indeed apply, provided there were no sublation of this [designation] by those other rules.
[However, the locative] denotes the locus of the action by way of the agent or the object.

Although the intended meaning of the locative case prescribed under the governing rule *kārake* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.23) is simply "the substratum of the action," nevertheless, in this context, there is indeed the status of being that substratum by way of the agent and the object. Nor should it be argued that even so, there would still be a confusion [of categories], because the distinction is maintained through the difference in the defining relata (*nirūpaka*).

The meaning of the accusative case is the locus as determined by the fruit (*phala*); the meaning of the instrumental case, however, is [the locus] as determined by the operation (*vyāpāra*); and the meaning of the locative case is [the locus] as determined by the operation of the agent or the object. Thus, in cases such as *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("he cooks in a pot"), *bhūtale vasati* ("he dwells on the ground"), and *kaṭe śete* ("he lies on a mat"), these constructions are justified.
And it has been said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "That which indirectly sustains the action, being separated from the agent and the object..."

"The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is traditionally held to be that which assists in the accomplishment of an action," so it is said. Furthermore, this locus is of three kinds: the contiguous (*aupaśleṣika*), the objective (*vaiṣayika*), and the pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*). Examples are: "He sleeps on a mat" (*kaṭe śete*), "He dwells with his teacher" (*gurau vasati*), "There is a desire for liberation" (*mokṣe icchāsti*), and "Oil is in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*). This is clearly explained in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *saṃhitāyām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.72).

The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamyartha*) is the limit (*avadhi*). This is based on the rule "the ablative is used for the *apādāna*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.29). Furthermore, according to the rule "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) during separation (*apāya*) is the *apādāna*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.24)—which means that the *apādāna* is the limit (*avadhibhūta*) with respect to the separation, which is the action that produces it—the sense is that it is the limit. This is the definition of the limit according to the perspective of the *Vākyapadīya*.
And it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "That which remains indifferent during a departure— whether moving or stationary—
is called the *apādāna* (ablative), because it is fixed and not involved in that [action]."
Since the horse is certainly falling from that which it falls,
the wall or other such object is likewise called "certain" (dhruva) with respect to the falling of that horse.
Although both rams are unstable when the disjunction is produced by the actions of both,
the two actions are nevertheless intended to be distinguished and established as separate therein.
"The status of being a limit (avadhitva) with respect to the respective actions of each of the two rams is distinct for each;
likewise, the status of being an agent (kartṛtva) with respect to their own respective actions is distinct for each.

This is the meaning [of the verse]. Regarding the term *apāye*—it refers to the action that causes separation (*viśleṣa*). *Udāsīnaḥ* means "not the locus" (*anāśrayaḥ*). *Atadāveśāt* means "because of not being the locus of that action. Thus, the result is: "being the locus of separation while not being the locus of the action that causes separation. In the example "the leaf falls from the tree," the phrase beginning with *satyam* ("while not being... is included to exclude the leaf [from being considered a limit].

In the case of "he falls from the running horse," the horse is the cause of the disjunction because it is the substratum of the action [of running]. However, in the case of "he falls from the horse that is falling from the wall," although the horse is indeed the substratum of the action that produces the disjunction, this does not contradict the definition; thus he says, "from which horse. The intended meaning is that the phrase must be qualified by "provided it is not the substratum of the action that causes that disjunction. Likewise, since it is not the substratum of the action residing in the horse, the wall and other such objects also possess the status of being *dhruva* (fixed/stable); thus he says, "of that too."

Anticipating the objection that in a case of separation produced by the action of both [agents], since the separation is one and the same, there would be no basis for the action that causes that disjunction, and thus the expression "two rams moving away from each other" would be impossible, the author provides the solution: "Both... He explains with the words "from the other ram": just as in the case of a stationary ram moving away from a second ram, the stationary ram possesses the status of a fixed point (*dhruva*) by taking the action of the departing ram, so too here, despite the oneness of the separation, because the actions are distinct, the other [ram] possesses the status of a fixed point by taking the action of one [of them].

Accordingly, it must be stated that "the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative) with respect to a particular action consists in being the locus of the separation [resulting from] that action, while not being the locus of the action that produces that separation. Furthermore, in this context, "action" refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and not merely physical motion (*spanda*). Consequently, the expression "the cloth falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣād vastraṃ patati*) is logically consistent even when the cloth possesses a separation produced by an action directed toward the tree. This explains that the previously mentioned definition does not involve being denoted by a case-ending (*vibhakti*).

In reality, it appears that this much is not what is denoted by the ablative (*pañcamī*), but rather it is merely the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the limit (*avadhi*). This is because, as in the case of the meaning of the accusative (*dvitīyā*), there is no possibility of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in usage; thus, its inclusion within the scope of the denotable content (*vācyakoṭi*) is impossible due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). Nor should one suspect that, even so, the expression "it flows from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt syandate*) would be improper; for this is accepted just like "he has moved from his seat" (*āsanāccalitaḥ*) or "he has departed from the kingdom" (*rājyāccalitaḥ*). By this, the fallacious solution—which claims that the cognition of the status of the *apādāna* (ablative point) produced by the ablative suffix requires the presence of a verbal root denoting an action with an object (*sakarmaka*)—is also refuted.

Even so, the expression "vṛkṣāt tyajati" (he leaves from the tree) would still be unavoidable; for since the designation of *apādāna* (ablative source) is superseded by the designation of *karman* (object), the use of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) would be impossible. If, however, it is established by experience that there is no comprehension when such a usage is made through error, then one must state that the cognition produced by a verbal root other than *tyaj* and its synonyms is the cause for the cognition of *apādānatva* generated by the fifth case. In expressions such as "balāhakād vidyotate" (it flashes forth from the cloud), the word "niḥsṛtya" (having emerged) is to be supplied. In the case of "rūpaṃ rasāt pṛthak" (form is distinct from taste), however, one should understand the *apādānatva* to be mentally constructed, or else the fifth case is used according to the rule "pṛthag-vinā."
And this threefold nature of the ablative is as follows:
some have their scope explicitly indicated, while others have their scope implied.
And that which has an implied action; thus, the ablative (apādāna) is said to be threefold.

Thus, according to the *Vākyapadīya*, [the ablation] is threefold: 1. "That in which the motion (*gati*) is directly indicated by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is called *nirdiṣṭaviṣaya* (indicated object). For example: *aśvāt patati* ("he falls from the horse"). 2. "That in which the verbal root expresses its own meaning as being subordinate to the meaning of another root is called *upāttaviṣaya* (appropriated object). For example: *balāhakād vidyotate* ("it flashes from the cloud"). Here, the root *dyuti* ("to flash") functions with flashing as subordinate to the act of emerging. 3. "That in which an action is required [to be supplied] is the last [type]. For example: *kuto bhavān* ("from where are you? [answering: *pāṭaliputrāt* ("from Pāṭaliputra"). Here, the connection must be made by supplying the sense of "going" (*gamana*). This is the meaning of the fourth case (*caturthy-artha*).

The object of reference (*uddeśya*) is the meaning of the dative case. For instance, according to the rule *sampradāne caturthī* (Pāṇini 2.3.13), and based on the rule *karmaṇā yamabhipraiti sa sampradānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.32)—which means that the factor (*kāraka*) which one intends to reach by means of the object (*karman*), i.e., by means of it acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*), is the recipient (*sampradāna*)—it follows that the object of reference is what is intended.

This very state is being-remnant (*śeṣitva*). Furthermore, it has been established in the *Pūrvatantra* that being-remnant (*śeṣatva*) consists in being the object of a desire directed toward that [principal]. For this very reason, in the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] beginning with "The handing over of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is like the throwing away" (4.2.6), it was determined that the handing over of the staff—enjoined by the rule, "When the Soma has been purchased, he gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa"—is not a disposal (*pratipatti*), but rather a primary act (*arthakarma*) based on the force of the dative case ending.

The statement "one gives a garment to the washerman" (*rajakāya vastraṃ dadāti*) is indeed accepted, as seen in examples from the *Mahābhāṣya* such as "the teacher Khaṇḍika gives a slap to his pupil" (*khaṇḍika upādhyāyaḥ śiṣyāya capeṭāṃ dadāti*).

However, the authors of the *Vṛtti*, explaining the term *sampradāna* according to its etymological meaning—as that to which something is properly given (*samyak pradīyate yasmai tat sampradānam*)—and thus describing its scope as extending to the point where one's own ownership ceases, say only "the garment of the washerman" (*rajakasya vastram*).
There are three types of *sampradāna*.
And this [object],
being desired by the agent for the sake of the action, is a factor of renunciation because it is not rejected;
furthermore, it attains the status of a recipient (sampradāna) through instigation or consent.

According to the *Vākyapadīya*, [the instigator] is of three kinds: first, as in "he offers an oblation to the Sun"; here the Sun neither requests, nor consents, nor refuses. The impeller is exemplified by "he gives a cow to the Brahmin. The consenter is exemplified by "he gives a cow to the teacher. This establishes that the case-endings denote the substratum (*dharmī*).

In all these cases, the relation [between the meanings] is one of identity between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix, because case-endings (*vibhakti*) denote the substratum (*dharmin*). For if they denoted only the property (*dharma*), there would result a violation of the natural sense of the rule "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.2), and because we observe this same principle in the case of *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes whose meanings include the object. Furthermore, in *bahuvrīhi* compounds where the second case and so on are the meaning—as in "one who has obtained water" (*prāptodakaḥ*)—we find that they denote the substratum. This is also supported by the *Mahābhāṣya*: "The meanings of the nominal endings (*sup*) are the object and so forth, as well as number; and the same applies to the verbal endings (*tiṅ*). This is the general direction of the argument.
Regarding the view that case-endings (*vibhakti*) denote properties (*dharma*):

since the substratum (*āśraya*) is already obtained by the base (*prakṛti*) itself, it is not denoted by the case-ending; rather, only the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatvamātra*) is denoted. And that very [state] serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) through identity (*tādātmya*). Furthermore, for the instrumental case (*karaṇatṛtīyā*), the operation (*vyāpāra*) is also [denoted]; for the ablative (*pañcamī*), mere separation (*vibhāga*); and for the dative (*caturthī*), mere status as the intended goal (*uddeśyatvamātra*).

Intending to show that for this very reason even the *Akṛtyadhikaraṇa* is not contradicted, he says: "Or rather, it is power (*śakti*) itself. The words "of all six" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. According to the rule *śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.50), the genitive case expresses mere relation (*sambandha-mātra*). However, in the case of the genitive of the kārakas, it is power itself; so much suffices.

Because the *bhāṣya* on the rule *saptamīpañcamyau kārakamadhye* (Pāṇini 2.3.7) shows the position that "capacity (*śakti*) is the *kāraka*," the understanding in the sentence "Devadatta’s cow is being given by me with my hand from the house to the Brahmin in the Gaṅgā" is as follows: there is an operation residing in me, which has the hand as its instrument, the Gaṅgā as its locus, which produces a separation residing in the house, is intended for the Brahmin, and is conducive to a renunciation whose locus is non-different from that cow which is related to Devadatta. This is according to the aforementioned manner.
[It is argued that] there is an impropriety in resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Demonstrating the proof for this, he addresses the Naiyāyikas and others who speak with much confusion, asserting that in expressions such as "he knows the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), the secondary nominal suffix (*dvitīyā*) has *viṣayatā* (objectness) as its denotation. He says: "The case-endings [denote] the object, etc. The intended meaning is this:
"The meanings of the case-endings (*sup*) are the object and so forth, as well as number; likewise, those of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*)."
The rule is established there, or rather, the rule applies to those things under discussion.

From the *Vārttika* and its *Bhāṣya*, the fact that the object (*karman*) and so forth are denotable meanings (*vācyatā*), as well as the restriction thereof, are obtained. To explain: through the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of [the rules] "svaujasamauṭ" (Pā. Sū. 4.1.2), "karmaṇi dvitīyā" (Pā. Sū. 2.3.2), "dvayekayordvivacanaikavacane" (Pā. Sū. 1.4.22), and so on; and [furthermore] of "laḥ karmaṇi ca" (Pā. Sū. 3.4.69), "lasya" (Pā. Sū. 3.4.77), "tip-tas-jhi" (Pā. Sū. 3.4.79), and "tānyekavacanadvivacana... (Pā. Sū. 1.4.101), etc., the denotability of the object and so forth, as well as their respective numbers, is established.

Likewise, that restriction is found to be twofold: the restriction of words (śabda-niyama), such as "the second [case-ending] is used only for the object (karman)," or "the third [case-ending] is used only for the instrument (karaṇa)," and so forth; and the restriction of meaning (artha-niyama), such as "only the second [case-ending] is used for the object," or "only the third [case-ending] is used for the instrument. Since figurative usage (lakṣaṇā) and the like—which contradict the established restrictions—are causes of ungrammaticality (asādhutva), they certainly fall under the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" during sacrificial rites. Therefore, even by one's own will, figurative usage is of no use regarding case-endings.
For this very reason, there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) in the case of a case-ending; such is the usage of the elder Naiyāyikas—this is the direction [of the argument]. || 24 ||
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of case-terminations (*subarthanirṇaya*) in the *Śrīvaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*. (3)
Now follows the determination of the meaning of names.
Regarding the presentation of various positions concerning the object of the name and its meaning,
he states the name and its meaning: "One, two, three, then four, and likewise five."
"All these positions regarding the meaning of names have been examined in the treatise. (25)
The referent of a name is either an individual or a genus;

the referent of a name is one genus, because it is more appropriate for that alone to be the denoted meaning due to parsimony, whereas if multiple individuals were the denoted meaning, there would be prolixity.

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) because individuals are also unitary each; for if one were to accept the expressive power (*śakti*) in only a single individual, then in other individuals it would have to be through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and the relation [of the word] would be "having as its substratum that which is inherent in itself," which is cumbersome (*gaurava*). But with the universal (*jāti*), the relation is simply "having a common substratum," which is parsimonious (*lāghava*). Furthermore, since the universal alone is the denoted meaning (*vācya*)—in accordance with the maxim that "that which is not grasped cannot serve as a qualifier" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*)—it is logical to prefer this over the view that the qualified individual is the denoted meaning; the cognition of the individual, however, occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And thus, the application of case-suffix meanings (*vibhaktyartha*) therein is also justified. This is the direction of the argument. The individual is the denoted meaning of the noun (*nāmārtha*).

Alternatively, the meaning of the word *eka* is simply the individual (*vyakti*) alone; for even in the view that the individual alone is the referent, both the mention of the suffix *aṇ* and the rule of *ekaśeṣa* are established within this very system. This is indeed logical, because in linguistic usage, the term is understood to refer precisely to the individual. Furthermore, since the delimiting property of the relation (*sambandhitāvacchedaka*)—that is, the genus—is one, the power (*śakti*) [of the word] is also one, and thus there is no complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor should it be suspected that, in this way, even "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) would be the denotable meaning because it is the delimiting factor of the denotability (śakyatāvacchedakatva); for, according to the maxim "that which is not grasped as a qualifier [cannot be the qualified]," one might argue that pot-ness itself should be the denotable meaning. However, such a suspicion is unfounded, because even though it is not the cause, it can serve as the delimiting factor of causality; and just as there is the delimiting factor of being the thing-to-be-defined (lakṣyatāvacchedakatva) even in what is not the actual thing-to-be-defined, so too is this possible here. As it has been said:

"For although entities are infinite, by making one of them a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa), the word's relation [to its meaning] becomes easy to establish, and it will not be subject to deviation."
The intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is that the meaning of a name consists of two [categories];
however, in reality, as it is said: "For one for whom the form (ākṛti) is the word-meaning, the substance (dravya) is not not the word-meaning."

The meaning expressed is more specific than that of the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, this is the intended sense of the word "one" (*ekam*): in the cognition of the word's power (*śakti*), the universal (*jāti*) alone is the single delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by way of being its object. Thus, in the case of a cognition qualified by "pot-ness," the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is such that the cause is the cognition of the power of the word as residing in "pot-ness" where "pot-ness" is not presented as a further qualifier (*anyāprakāraka*). This and more has been elaborated upon in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. Having this in mind, he says "the pair" (*dvikam*), meaning the universal and the individual (*jāti-vyaktī*). The resolution of the contradiction with the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as before.

The term "trika" means the triad of genus (*jāti*), individual (*vyakti*), and gender (*liṅga*). Regarding grammatical gender (*liṅga*), its residing within the word and its nature as a quality are as follows:

the state of equilibrium among the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is neuter gender; their predominance is masculine gender; and their diminution is feminine gender. This resides in and is denoted by each respective word; it is precisely by taking up these contradictory attributes that words such as *taṭa* (bank) are differentiated.
The conventional usage of multiple genders for certain words, however, arises from the superimposition of non-difference among words due to their having identical phonetic sequences (*anupūrvī*).

Thus, in the word *padārtha*, there is only masculinity; in the word *vyakti*, only femininity; and in the word *vastu*, only neuter gender. Consequently, the usage "this is a *padārtha*," "this is a *vyakti*," and "this is a *vastu*" occurs everywhere, and the forms *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam* are likewise justified.
Gender is construed as a qualifier that delimits the meaning (*arthaparicchedaka*).

And that gender follows as a qualifier by way of delimiting the meaning; thus, one must discern that the injunctions such as "the animal is not [used] in the feminine" and "with the animal" do not employ goats and the like as subordinate elements (*aṅga*). Nor should it be suspected that the gender expressed by words such as *paśu* is common [to both genders], in the same way as the gender expressed by words such as *vyakti*; for while that may be possible because the word *vyakti* is eternally feminine, there is no evidence for the word *paśu* being eternally masculine—as in:
"Like a thief moving in a cave, [he saw] the animal" (*Ṛgveda* 1.12.65).

Furthermore, because such [usage] is seen in the Veda, for example in *paśve nṛbhyo yathā gave* (RV 1.3.26), and because it is established in the fourth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā that in the injunction *paśunā yajeta*, both singularity and masculinity are intended to be significant, such that the sacrifice is not to be performed with multiple animals or with a female animal.

In reality, however, since grammar has determined that words ending in the suffix *up* possess the masculine gender in the absence of a specific rule to the contrary—and since it is stated in the Vedabhāṣya regarding the forms *jas* and so forth that "in the Veda there is optionally the non-occurrence of *nāb*"—it is established that the word *paśu* is invariably masculine. In the present case, the determination is made by the very principle of "the goat [is meant] because of the wording of the mantra," for in the mantra it is heard: "of the omentum and fat of the goat."

In that context, the phrase "of the goat" (*chāgasya*) is impossible when applied to a female goat; thus, there arises a determination of its being masculine. This has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. "The fourfold" refers to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*);
"the fourfold" means the triad accompanied by number.

The "pentad" is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); that is to say, the pentad [consisting of gender, number, case-role, and the object itself] together with the fourfold [set]. Now, one might object: "By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is the suffix alone that expresses that [meaning], since gender and the rest are presented by that very [suffix]; therefore, there is no evidence for their being expressed by the base (*prakṛti*). This is true; however, because understanding occurs even for one who does not know the suffix in cases such as *dadhi paśya* ("look at the curd")—which are devoid of suffixes—it is postulated that the expressive power belongs to the base alone, and furthermore, because the grammatical rules on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) are observed to apply to the base alone.

For this very reason, there is no insistence on these alternative views, since it is more logical that the suffix itself possesses the expressive power (*vācakatā*). This is because both positions are expounded even in the *Vākyapadīya*: "The case-endings may be either indicators (*dyotikā*) or expressers (*vācikā*) of duality and the other numbers."

In this treatise, the derivation [of words] is intended to be illustrated in many places; however, it is most clearly demonstrated in the section on "homogeneous suffixes" (*sarūpa-sūtra*) and elsewhere. || 25 ||
The six categories constitute the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Sound (*śabda*) is also the meaning of the nominal stem;
for sound indeed appears in verbal cognition.
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of sound.
All knowledge appears as if permeated by sound.
This is because of the statement of the learned authorities:

"In cases such as 'pronounce Viṣṇu,' since the pronunciation of the meaning is impossible, and since verbal cognition would otherwise be inconsistent without the word being the object [of that cognition], that [word] is also the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha). Nor can this be resolved through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā), because established metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā) is not distinct from primary denotation (śakti); furthermore, in examples such as "pronounce jabagaḍadaśa," no primary meaning is apprehended, and thus a metaphorical indication—defined as a relation with the primary meaning—cannot be apprehended either.

Considering that an unknown mode of operation would be useless, and that the grammatical correctness of imitating colloquial words—such as in the expression "utter the word *gāvaḥ* (cows)"—is universally accepted, and further considering that, due to the absence of primary denotative power (*śakti*) in those cases, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is impossible according to the opponent's own system, [the author] states that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is sixfold in some instances:
"If there were a desire to express the word itself as distinct [from its meaning], then it would appear in that way.
Otherwise, even though established by the auditory organs and so forth, that word does not appear as a separate object. (26)

If there is an intention to express the difference between the original (anukārya) and the imitation (anukaraṇa), then the word itself is the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha). If there is no intention to express the difference, then even though it is presented by the auditory organ and other senses, it appears as if it were an object [of denotation]. The particle "api" indicates a reason; the sense is that it appears because it has been presented. This is the underlying point: when there is a difference between the original and the imitation, since the original is not presented by the word, a denotative power (śakti) must be admitted to establish it. When there is non-difference, however, because the object is the cause of its own perception, the status of being an object of verbal cognition is established by taking the presentation produced by the word—which is of the nature of the word's own perception—as the means.

Even if, in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the cause [of verbal cognition] is held to be only the presentation of a word (*padopasthiti*) produced by its linguistic function (*vṛtti*), nevertheless, there is no inconsistency here because the property of possessing a linguistic function (*vṛttimattva*) exists in [the word] as its substratum (*āśrayatā*). It is faultless to postulate that only that which possesses a linguistic function—by way of either the relation of being a determiner (*nirūpakatā*) or the relation of being a substratum (*āśrayatā*)—is the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). This is because a relation is determined by both relata; and furthermore, just as an object is known through a word, the word itself can also be known as the signifier of that object.
As it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Like light, there are two powers: that of being the apprehended (*grāhyatva*) and that of being the apprehender (*grāhakatva*)."
"In the same way, these [sounds] of all words exist separately.
Thus, it is said that "the meaning is not manifested by words without disregarding their status as objects";
this refers to the non-difference between the original (anukārya) and the imitation (anukaraṇa).
In this context, as a corollary, he states the proof for the position that the original object (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*) are non-different:
"For this very reason, [the form] 'gāv'—as in 'bhū sattāyām'—is considered neither a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) nor a word (*pada*), yet it is regarded as grammatically correct. (27)

He says this because words such as ‘*bhū*’ [in the rule] ‘*bhū sattāyām*’ (*DhP* 1.1), being words of imitation (*anukaraṇaśabda*), are not distinct from that which is imitated (*anukārya*). Therefore, since they lack possessiveness of meaning (*arthavattva*), the rules beginning with ‘*arthavad adhātuḥ*’ (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.2.45) do not apply; consequently, they possess neither the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) nor the status of a word (*pada*). Nevertheless, their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is established.

Otherwise, there would result a lack of correctness due to the violation of rules such as ‘*pratyayaḥ*’ (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.1), ‘*paraśca*’ (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.2), and the prohibition ‘*apadaṃ na prayuñjīta*’. This is the meaning. || 27 ||
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of nouns in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra composed by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Raṅgojibhaṭṭa. 4.
Now follows the determination of the expressive power of compounds (samāsa-śakti-nirṇaya).
Regarding the classification of compounds,
he divides them as follows:

The wise should understand that compound (samāsa) is of six kinds: [a word] ending in a *sup* suffix with another word ending in a *sup* suffix; with a *tiṅ* suffix; with a noun (*nāman*); with a verbal root (*dhātu*); [a word] ending in a *tiṅ* suffix with another word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix; and [a word] ending in a *sup* suffix with a word ending in a *sup* suffix. (28)
The pair of words "supām supā" refers to that which ends in a *sup* suffix; examples include *rājapuruṣaḥ* and the like.

Regarding "supām tiṅā," the first member ends in a *sup* suffix and the second member ends in a *tiṅ* suffix; examples are *paryabhūṣayat* and *anuvyacalat*. The compound is formed by the Vārttika: "There is also a compound with a *tiṅ*-ending word that possesses a motion [meaning] and is accented on the first syllable."

The form *kumbhakāraḥ* and others are derived from nominal stems (*supām nāmnām*). The compound is formed by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). This occurs prior to the application of case-endings (*subutpatteḥ prāk*) by the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*): "There is a statement regarding the compounding of prefixes (*gati*), agents (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) with primary derivatives (*kṛt*) before the arising of case-endings. Here, the meaning is that this occurs before the case-ending arises on the final member (*uttarapada*). Otherwise, in forms such as *carmakrītī*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would not be possible.

The compound of nominal suffixes (*sup*) with a verbal root (*dhātu*) results in a form consisting of the root alone, not a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), as per the Vārttika: *kvib-vaci-praccha-āyata-stu-kaṭapru-ju-śrīṇāṃ dīrghaś-ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.178], yielding examples such as *kaṭapruḥ* and *āyatastūḥ*.

The compound of finite verbs (*tiṅ*) with finite verbs includes forms such as *pibatakhādatā* and *pacatabhṛjjatā*, according to the rule within the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group: *ākhyātam ākhyātena kriyāsātatye* [Pāṇini 2.1.72].

A verbal form (*tiṅanta*) preceded by a nominal stem (*subanta*) and followed by a nominal stem—such as *jahistambaḥ*—is derived from the rule for the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group: "The word *jahi*, when used with an object, frequently [forms a compound] in the sense of repetition, and it denotes the agent.

This sixfold type of compound has been explained in the *Bhāṣya* through a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *saha supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), as is clear from the *Śabdakaustubha* and other works. || 28 ||

The fact that the definitions such as "that in which the meaning of the prior member is predominant" (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*) are merely conventional is established by the Bhāṣya itself; having demonstrated this distinction, he shows that the division stated by the ancient grammarians is subject to under-extension (*avyāpti*), over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and other defects, and that their definition is likewise merely conventional: "The statement that 'the compound is fourfold' is a conventional claim, and so is the other."
And this [topic], which concerns the predominance of the meaning of the prior member and so forth, is as follows: || 29 ||
On account of its prior occurrence, that too is established as being like a line-drawn gavaya and so forth. || 29½ ||

It is fourfold, according to the division into *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, *dvandva*, and *bahuvrīhi*. This is a general statement, as it does not include examples such as *bhūtapūrvaḥ*, *dṛnbhūḥ* (or *kārābhūḥ*), *āyatastūḥ*, and "like word and meaning" (*vāgarthāviva*).

Likewise, the definitions that "an *avyayībhāva* is primarily the meaning of the first member," "a *tatpuruṣa* is primarily the meaning of the final member," "a *dvandva* is primarily the meaning of both members," and "a *bahuvrīhi* is primarily the meaning of a word other than those members" are merely general rules, because they mutually deviate in cases such as *unmattagaṅgam*, *sūpaprati*, *ardhapippalī*, *dvitrāḥ*, and *śaśakuśapalāśam*.

For instance: in the case of the *avyayībhāva* compound *unmattagaṅgam*, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) because the meaning of the prior member is not predominant; furthermore, there is over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *bahuvrīhi* because the meaning of another word is predominant, owing to the rule "and when denoting the meaning of another word, provided it is a technical name" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.1.21). In the case of the *avyayībhāva* compound *sūpaprati*, there is over-pervasion of the definition of *tatpuruṣa* because the meaning of the subsequent member is predominant, and there is non-pervasion of the *avyayībhāva* itself, owing to the rule "with *prati* in the sense of measure, [it forms a compound] with a case-inflected word" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.1.9).

In the *tatpuruṣa* compound “*ardhapippalī*,” because there is predominance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārthaprādhānya*), there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to *avyayībhāva* compounds and under-extension (*avyāpti*) to *tatpuruṣa* compounds, due to the rule “*ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*” (Pāṇini 2.2.2). The same should be observed for examples such as “*pūrvakāyaḥ*. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound “*dvitrāḥ*,” because there is predominance of the meanings of both members, there is over-extension to *dvandva* compounds and under-extension to *bahuvrīhi* compounds. In *dvandva* compounds such as “*śaśakuśapalāśam*,” because there is predominance of the collective meaning (*samāhāra*) as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), there would be over-extension to *bahuvrīhi* compounds and over-extension to *dvandva* compounds; this is the intended sense.

In our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, one should observe that "the status of being an *avyayībhāva* consists in being recited under the heading of *avyayībhāva*" and so forth. He states that these [definitions] are impossible, beginning with the words "due to their being based on what has already occurred" (*bhautapūrvyāt*). Just as the tail and other features residing in a "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavaya*) do not constitute the defining characteristics of a real animal, so too these [definitions] do not constitute the definition of a compound (*samāsa*). The intended meaning is that their capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatā*) would be exactly like that [of the line-drawn gavaya]. || 29½ ||

In response to the doubt that, under the *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandonment of its own meaning) view, the systematic arrangement regarding the predominance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārthaprādhānya*) and so forth is possible, [the author] says: "Now, it is indeed easy to state the predominance of the first member and so forth within a compound. For instance, although many views were expressed by the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, they ultimately result in only two: the *jahatsvārthā* and *ajahatsvārthā* views, which take the form of *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning) and *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy), respectively. With this in mind, considering the doubt that the aforementioned arrangement is not impossible under the *ajahatsvārthā* view, he says:"
The examination of *jahatsvārthā* and *ajahatsvārthā*:
there are two types of function (*vṛtti*), namely *jahatsvārthā* and *ajahatsvārthā*, and these two are each further divided into three kinds. (30)
For the determination of the denotable object consists of difference, relation, or both. || 30½ ||

That [theory] in which [the words] abandon their own individual meanings is called *jahatsvārthā*. The meaning is that, just as phonemes have no meaning in a word, so too the constituent words have no meaning in a compound (*vṛtti*). The underlying idea is this: since the cognition (understanding) of a person qualified by a king can arise through the power of the compound itself, there is no need to assume that the two words "king" and "person" possess the capacity to convey that same meaning once again, just as the words "bull" and so on do not [convey the meaning] in compounds such as *vṛṣabha* or *yāvaka*.

Otherwise, just as in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), the king would exist independently due to the presence of the word "king," there would arise the undesirable consequence that "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*) could just as well mean "the man of a wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).
Regarding the term *ajahat*: that [function] in which words do not abandon their own meaning is *ajahatsvārthā*.
This concludes the examination of the position of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāpakṣa*).
