The intention is as follows: in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), there is no additional *śakti* (expressive power), because there is no evidence for its postulation (*kalpaka*), and because the postulation of such a power is refuted by the principle of complexity (*gaurava*), since the meaning can be presented simply from the already established words "king" and so forth. Furthermore, the abandonment of an established *śakti* would itself have to be postulated without any authoritative basis (*aprāmāṇika*). Thus, through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, the cognition of the qualified meaning arises precisely through the established *śakti*.
This very position, known as the *vyapekṣā-pakṣa*, was stated by the authors of the *Bhāṣya* as an alternative view.

Furthermore, in this view, there is no contingency of the qualifier "of the prosperous one" (*ṛddhasya*) being construed with the compound, because of the Vārttika: "There is no composition [of a compound] with qualifiers; nor is there connection with a qualifier for that which has already been composed. Thus, the intention is that for those who maintain this view, the systematic classification—such as "the former member's meaning is predominant"—is well-founded, since the meanings of both the preceding and succeeding members exist. Each individual type of composition (*vṛtti*) is likewise threefold.

In this context, he also defines the different types of function (*vṛtti*) by the words "those two," etc. Both functions are of three kinds, because the denoted meaning (*vācya*) is of three kinds. He states the denoted meaning itself with the words "difference," etc. "Difference" (*bheda*) means mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Thus, in cases such as "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), the understanding is "one who is distinct from those belonging to non-kings. If this were not denoted, then just as one says "the king’s man is handsome," one could also say "the king’s man belongs to Devadatta. The point is that since it is denoted, there is no such usage because of the contradiction involved.

The verbal cognition is simply "one who possesses a connection with a king," while the difference (from others) arises at a subsequent time; with this intention, he says "the relation" (*saṃsarga*). Considering that there would be no basis for determining which [of the two] is primary, and that the usage "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*) would result even in the case of one who has no owner, he says "or both" (*ubhayaṃ vā*), meaning both are denoted. Thus, the understanding is: "this person is distinct from those not belonging to a king and possesses a connection with a king. || 30½ ||

The demonstration of the distinctness of the power of a compound (*samāsa-śakti*) from the power of a sentence consisting of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā-rūpa-vākya-śakti*) is thus contrary to the reasoning and the *Bhāṣya* of the *Vyapekṣā-vāda*. Consequently, the general rule (*utsarga*) based upon that—namely, "the first member is predominant" (*pūrvapadārtha-pradhāna*) and so forth—is also untenable. However, with the intention that even this general rule is indicative only through a traditional succession according to the maxim of the "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhā-gavaya*), he provides the following resolution:
"In a compound, indeed, there is a distinct power, just like the word *paṅkaja*. (31)
If the accomplishment of many functions and properties were achieved through words alone, there would be great prolixity; therefore, the principle of unification (ekārthībhāva) is resorted to.

The term *samāsa* (compound) is an illustration for all *vṛtti*s (grammatical formations) in general. This is because the meaning of the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.1)—as understood from the Bhāṣya—is that any formation such as a compound (*samāsa*) and so forth, which is prescribed with reference to a word (*pada*), is "samartha," meaning it is capable of expressing the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) and is thus grammatically correct (*sādhu*). Furthermore, the status of being a rule prescribed with reference to a word is established in all five types of *vṛtti*s;

indeed, this status of being a rule prescribed with reference to a word exists in all five *vṛtti*s, namely: primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), elliptical formations (*ekaśeṣa*), and verbal roots ending in *san*-type affixes (*sanādyanta-dhātu*).

The Refutation of the Theory of Mutual Expectation (*vyapekṣāvādakhaṇḍana*): With the intention that the critique of those proponents of mutual expectation (*vyapekṣāvādins*) who do not accept specific capacities (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) actually serves as a proof for [the existence of] such capacities, he says: "Just like the word *paṅkaja*" (*paṅkajaśabdavat*). If even the agent of the production of mud (*paṅkajanikartṛ*) were presented through etymological derivation (*yoga*) alone, then even in that case, a collective capacity (*samudāyaśakti*) would not be established. Nor should it be argued that such a capacity is postulated for the sake of presenting [the object] in the form of a lotus (*padmatva*), because in words such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows") as well, the postulation of that [collective capacity] would be necessary for the sake of presenting [the meaning] as an owner (*svāmitva*). If it is argued that such presentation occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, then that can be equally asserted for the word *paṅkaja*. The same applies to the word *rathakāra* ("chariot-maker").

And likewise, in the case of the injunction, "During the rainy season, a *rathakāra* should establish the sacred fires," the sense is that since the rule can be explained as referring to Brāhmaṇas and others through its established etymological meaning (*yoga*) without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it would be improper to assume a specific caste as the qualified agent and thereby postulate a previously unknown Vedic text (*apūrva-vidyā*).
This demonstrates the prolixity (*gaurava*) in the view that [the word] depends on multiple factors (*vyapekṣā-pakṣa*),
wherein many properties of the function must be established by means of verbal statements.

He states another argument for proof: "of many," etc. The meaning is that there is prolixity (*gaurava*) in establishing the properties of a word-meaning—such as its connection with qualifiers, gender, number, and so forth—by means of their respective linguistic expressions. This is the underlying idea: if one does not accept specific capacities (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), then just as in the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), there would also be a connection with qualifiers and so on in the case of "king-man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), because the independent presentation (*svatantra-upasthiti*) exists even through the word "king. Furthermore, the rule regarding optionality (*vibhāṣā-vacana*) must be formulated to prevent the restriction [that applies] to compounds.

One might raise the objection: "Is it not the case that, because of the rule *saviśe�ṣaṇānām*, there is no connection with qualifiers and the like, and that the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) has already been established? He resolves this doubt with the words *vacanair eva*. The Sūtra is indeed established by logic (*nyāya*). For, when there is a desire to express analytical expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), the result is a sentence (*vākya*); whereas when there is the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the result is a compound (*samāsa*). Since such a restriction on usage is possible through the very nature of things, the sense is that even the rule *saviśeṣaṇānām* is established by logic; for when a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) is involved, the king—being only a part of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśa*)—cannot be connected [with the qualifier]. Thus, it is established by logic.

For this very reason, having raised the position of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), the author of the Bhāṣya has also stated the following refutation: "Now, if semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists in mutual expectancy, then that specific distinction produced by 'becoming a single meaning' (*ekārthībhāva*) must be explained. || 32 ||

Likewise, in cases such as *dhavakhadirau* (the dhava and khadira trees), *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī), *gorathaḥ* (an ox-cart), *ghṛtaghaṭaḥ* (a jar of ghee), *guḍadhānāḥ* (barley mixed with molasses), *keśacūḍaḥ* (a crest of hair), *suvarṇālaṅkāraḥ* (gold ornament), *dvidaśāḥ* (twenty), and *saptaparṇāḥ* (a tree with seven leaves), one would have to state by explicit rule (*vācanika*) the meanings of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), departure (*niṣkrānta*), connection (*yukta*), fullness (*pūrṇa*), mixture (*miśra*), aggregate (*saṅghāta*), the elision of the suffix *suc* denoting modification (*vikāra*), and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), which would result in excessive complexity (*atigaurava*).

Thus, he states another objection: "Furthermore, there would be a prohibition of the particle *ca* and so forth, and the destruction of many grammatical derivations (*vyutpatti*) would have to be performed by you; whereas for us, that [derivation] is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*)—such is our position. (33)
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of [epithets] such as "dark as a rain-cloud" (*ghanaśyāma*) and "gait like that of a swan" (*haṃsagamana*), as well as those previously mentioned.
He states another fault—namely, the "shattering of many etymological derivations" (*bahuvyutpattibhañjana*)—as follows: "the shattering of many etymological derivations."

The intention is as follows: In the case of "citraguḥ" (the one possessing brindled cows), the cognition of ownership and so forth is established by experience. Nor is there metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here, because that is impossible in cases such as "prāptodako grāmaḥ" (the village reached by water). Even if one were to assume a metaphorical indication of the village as being related to the water—following the understanding that "the water is non-different from the agent who has reached [it]"—one still fails to obtain the meaning "the village is the object of the reaching whose agent is the water."

If it is argued that the suffix *kta* in *prāpta* (in *udakaprāpta*) has the agent as its primary meaning and functions as a *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the object, then—given the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that two words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) denote their referents as non-different (*abheda*)—the result would have to be "water non-different from the object of attainment" (*udakābhinnaprāptikarma*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of violating the rule regarding the non-difference of referents of words in apposition; furthermore, since "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), water cannot be construed with it as distinct through the relation of agency (*kartṛtā*).

Otherwise, in the case of "Devadatta is cooking" (*devadattaḥ pacyate*), since Devadatta could be construed as the agent through the relation of agency (*kartṛtā-sambandha*), the fault of non-construction (*ananvaya*) would not arise.

If it is argued that after the cognition "the attainment has the same agent as water," the village related to that [attainment] is indicated (*lakṣyate*), this is not so; for since attainment is the meaning of the verbal root, it is impossible for it to be the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) with respect to the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix *-kta*. This is because of the established rule (*vyutpatti*): "Between the meanings of the base and the suffix, the meaning of the suffix alone is predominant. Furthermore, if attainment were the qualificand in the word *prāpta*, then since it would be the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāmartha*), it would follow that it must be construed as non-different (*abheda-anvaya*) from "water."

The same should be understood in cases such as *ūḍharathaḥ* ("one who has brought a chariot"), *upahṛtapaśuḥ* ("one for whom an animal has been offered"), *uddhṛtaudanā* ("one from whose [pot] rice has been taken out"), and *bahupācikā* ("one who cooks much"). For here, one must admit that the understanding is: "the agent of the act of carrying whose object is the chariot," "the intended recipient of the act of offering whose object is the animal," "the limit of the act of taking out whose object is the rice," and "the locus of the agent of the act of cooking much. And according to the view that there is a distinct function (a whole-word power), the explanation is achieved through the very power of the composite expression *prāptodakaḥ* and so on, residing in that which is qualified by being the object of the arrival whose agent is water—just as the word *ghaṭa* resides in that which is qualified by the property of potness (*ghaṭatva*). This is the sense. || 33 ||

Regarding the *aṣaṣṭhyartha-bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound not involving the genitive case), he states another supporting argument: "In the case of an *aṣaṣṭhyartha-bahuvrīhi*, there is the burden of postulating a separate grammatical derivation (*vyutpattyantarakalpanā*)."
Since you possess the capacity for relinquishing what has been prepared, why do you not likewise postulate [the existence of] power? (34)

The demonstration that there is no justification for the theory of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in *bahuvrīhi* compounds such as *citragu* (the one who has brindled cows) with respect to the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) is as follows: In cases such as *citragu*, the cognition of the owner of the brindled cows cannot be accounted for without assuming a primary denotative power (*śakti*). Nor can it be explained by *lakṣaṇā*. For *lakṣaṇā* cannot reside in the word *citra* (brindled), because that would result in the erroneous cognition "the cow is the owner of the brindled [one]. Nor can it reside in the word *go* (cow), because that would result in the erroneous syntactic cognition "the owner of the cow is brindled. This is because the mere quality of being brindled constitutes only a part of the indicated object, and therefore the cow and so forth cannot logically enter into a relation with it.
Thus, the possibility of *lakṣaṇā* in the word *go* is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that, after the cognition of the relation between the two meanings presented by the respective powers—namely, "the cow non-different from variegated" (*citrābhinnā gauḥ*)—the owner of such a cow is indicated (*lakṣyate*) by the word *go* (cow). This is because there is no basis for determining (*vinigamanā-viraheṇa*) whether the word *go* or the word *citrapada* is the one that performs the indication. Nor should it be argued that the direct connection [of the primary meaning] with the word *go* is indeed the determining factor; for even so, in the case of bahuvrīhi compounds where the genitive sense is not expressed, such as *prāptodakaḥ* ("one who has obtained water") and *kṛtaviśvaḥ* ("one who has created the universe"), no determining factor would be available. This is because, since derivative (*yaugika*) words denote agents and so forth, there is no difference in their direct connection [to the compound's meaning]. Thus, the charge of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) against the word *go* is refuted.
The refutation of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in both words:

Nor is the Naiyāyika claim that "there is *lakṣaṇā* in both words" tenable, because it would entail the recurrence of the cognition (*bodha*). Nor can it be argued that there is no recurrence of the cognition because *lakṣaṇā* belongs to only one word at a time—since they mutually indicate the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*)—for even so, *lakṣaṇā* remains impossible due to the persistence of the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-viraha*).
[This concludes] the refutation of *lakṣaṇā* in the final word.

Nor should it be argued that [the suffix] belongs only to the final member, on the grounds of the requirement for the meaning of the suffix to connect [with that member], since there is a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meaning as residing in the word-meaning immediately preceding them; for if that were so, the formation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound would be impossible, because the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24) prescribes that multiple *sub*-ending words [form a compound] when they denote a meaning other than their own constituent members.

Furthermore, this being the case, one might as well assume that in words such as "ghaṭa" (pot), the denotative power belongs to the final letter alone, since the preceding letters could serve their purpose by indicating the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). If it is argued that this would result in the comprehension of the meaning upon hearing only the final letter, the same objection applies here: it would follow that the meaning is understood from hearing only the word "udaka" (water). This has been explained in detail elsewhere.

And thus, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is not present, one must assume a different etymological derivation; for the reason already stated, there is no other recourse but to assume a distinct denotative power (*śakti*). Furthermore, you have abandoned the established etymology [of assuming a power] by asserting that the formation is explained through an already established power. What, then, is the meaning of your statement? It is this: why should one not assume a power in every compound?
Regarding the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*) held by the modern Naiyāyikas and Mīmāṃsakas:

those Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others who maintain the theory of mutual expectancy hold that there is no power in a compound, because in expressions such as "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), the word "king" (*rāja*) and so forth—[retain their own individual meanings].
For the cognition "the person is non-different from that which is related to the king" is established by the very function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on relation.

For this very reason, since the king constitutes only a part of the referent of the word *rājñaḥ*, words such as "beautiful" cannot be construed with him. Nor does there arise the contingency of using particles like *iva* in cases such as *ghanaśyāmaḥ* ("dark as a cloud"), *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("departed from Kauśāmbī"), or *gorathaḥ* ("ox-cart"), because the use of words such as *krānta* ("gone") is impossible precisely when the meaning has already been expressed [by the compound].

Nor is the rule *vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.11) necessary, because it is possible to establish a restriction on usage such that the compound is employed when one intends to convey "a person non-different from one related to a king," whereas the analytical expression (*vigraha*) is used when one intends to convey "one who possesses a relation to a king. Furthermore, the analogy with the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") does not prove [the existence of] a primary denotative power (*śakti*), since understanding occurs even for one who is unaware of the powers of its constituent parts.

Furthermore, if the primary denotative power (*śakti*) is not apprehended, it is impossible for a cognition of a qualified object to arise from those words through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For this very reason, when the denotative power of words such as "king" is not apprehended, there is no comprehension in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man") or *citraguḥ* ("one who has variegated cows"). Nor should it be argued that even if secondary indication is possible in cases like *citraguḥ*, it is impossible in a Bahuvrīhi compound where the genitive case-meaning is absent, because that would entail the collapse of many established linguistic conventions; for in examples such as *prāptodakaḥ* ("to whom water has come"), secondary indication is accepted as residing in the word *udaka* itself.

Because the first member of a compound is etymological (yaugika), its indication (lakṣaṇā) is delayed, as it must be accomplished through the knowledge of the verbal root, the suffix, and their respective meanings; furthermore, this is due to the linguistic rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as residing in the object denoted by the immediately preceding word. In the case of words such as "ghaṭa" (pot), when a distinct power (śakti) is postulated, it is postulated for the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa), because it is the qualified entity alone that is the subject of the convention (saṅketa). Moreover, the capacity to convey meaning does not reside in each individual phoneme. In the present case, however, the distinction is that this power is postulated in the second member of the compound itself, so that the connection with the meaning of the suffix may be easily achieved through extreme proximity.
Furthermore, they state that even in words such as "ghaṭa" (pot), those who consider themselves Mīmāṃsakas have accepted that the final letter alone possesses the expressive power (*vācakatva*).
Regarding the refutation of the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*) by both the Neo-Naiyāyikas and the Mīmāṃsakas:
if one does not accept a primary significative power (*śakti*) in a compound (*samāsa*), it would follow that the compound cannot be considered a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

To this it is replied: if the capacity (*śakti*) were not admitted in a compound (*samāsa*), it would not receive the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and so forth, because it would lack possessiveness of meaning (*arthavattva*); for the rule "That which is meaningful, being neither a root nor an affix, is a nominal stem" (Pāṇini 1.2.45) would not apply. Nor can it be argued that the designation is established by the mention of "compound" in the rule "And kṛt-derivatives, taddhita-derivatives, and compounds" (Pāṇini 1.2.46), because the status of that mention as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*) has been clearly demonstrated in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*, as established by the *Mahābhāṣya*.

In a compound (samāsa), since there is an absence of expressive power (*śakti*), even *lakṣaṇā*—which consists of a relationship with the primary meaning—is impossible; consequently, the possession of a denotative meaning (*lākṣaṇikārthavattva*) is also impossible. Now, if one were to adopt the *tip-pratyāhāra* established in the Bhāṣya, beginning from "tiptasjhi" up to "ṅayossup," and formulate the rule simply as "that which is not a *tip* or a *prātipadika* [is a word]," then the two rules beginning with "arthavat" would be redundant. Furthermore, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) could then serve the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

If it is argued that, since the definition of a *prātipadika* is "that which is different from a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and a nominal suffix (*sup*"), this designation would apply to a compound as well; even so, because meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) is necessary to exclude the individual phonemes from receiving the name, the same deficiency regarding the non-extension of the term to compounds remains. Thus, the very operation consisting of the designation *prātipadika* implies meaningfulness, just as smoke implies fire.
Furthermore, in cases such as *citraguḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the case-role (karmatva) associated with the meaning of the suffix.

Furthermore, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence that in expressions such as *citragumānaya* ("bring the owner of brindled cows"), the accusative case-relation (*karmatva*) and so forth could not be construed [with the cow]. This is because of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes generate the cognition of their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), and because the suffix arises only after a qualified form, that qualified form alone constitutes the base. As for the claim that one should instead postulate a rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as residing in the proximate word-meaning—that is not correct, because it is contradicted by examples such as *upakumbham* ("near the jar") and *arddhapippalī* ("half a pepper"), where the meaning of the case-suffix is construed with the meaning of the preceding member of the compound.

Nor is mere proximity (*sannidhi*) sufficient even there, because what is intended is proximity through grammatical instruction (*ānuśāsanika*). Thus, whatever suffix is prescribed after a particular word conveys its own meaning as residing in the meaning of that word. And in the case of a compound, it must be stated that the grammatical instruction applies specifically after the compounded words, because by the rule *arthavat* (Pāṇini 1.2.45), only the composite whole is designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and the suffix is prescribed after that composite whole. Therefore, the claim that the meaning of the suffix is construed with the substratum of the base (*prakṛti*) is incorrect.

Now, if it is argued that one should simply postulate that "the meaning of the case-ending (vibhaktyartha) is construed with the locus of the base-meaning (prakṛtitva)," then there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the acts of bringing, seeing, and worshipping being construed with the mud, the staff, and the trident in such expressions as "bring the lotus" (*paṅkajam ānaya*), "see the staff-bearer" (*daṇḍinaṃ paśya*), and "worship the trident-bearer" (*śūlinaṃ pūjaya*); furthermore, in the case of "bring the non-pot" (*aghaṭam ānaya*), it would entail the construction of the act of bringing with the pot itself.

Nor is it the case that because sticks and the like function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with actions such as "bringing" in those instances; for if that were so, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that in expressions such as "blue from cooking" (*pākānnīlaḥ*) or "happy through merit" (*dharmāt sukhī*), the causality of "cooking" or "merit" could not be connected to the "blueness" or "happiness. Furthermore, if you argue that being the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatva*) is merely being an object of the cognition produced by it—and that this is not contradictory here—that is not correct. For in the sentence "see the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ paśya*), the status of being the meaning of the base by way of its linguistic function (*vṛtti*) is necessary in order to exclude space (*ākāśa*), which is presented [as a possible referent] from the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
A refutation of the claim that "the status of being the meaning of a base (*prakṛtyarthatva*) consists in being the qualificand of a presentation produced by a word preceding the suffix":

If it is argued that "the status of being the meaning of a base consists in being the qualificand of a presentation produced by a word preceding the suffix," this is not so; for in the sentence *gām ānayati kṛṣṇo daṇḍena* ("He brings the cow with a stick, Kṛṣṇa"), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*) being construed with Kṛṣṇa.

Furthermore, there is the burden of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating that the case-suffix following a compound conveys its own meaning as residing in the meaning of the constituent words being compounded.

If it is argued that the capacity of the case-ending following a compound to convey its own meaning is assumed with respect to the meanings of the constituent members being compounded, this is not so; for it is more reasonable to assume a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) than to resort to an unestablished assumption while abandoning an established etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. If one does not accept a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in a compound, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) in cases such as *rājapuruṣa*.

Furthermore, if one does not accept a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in compounds, there would be the undesirable consequence of a total lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya-prasaṅga*) in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man), *citraguḥ* (the owner of brindled cows), and *nīlotpalam* (the blue lotus). This is because even if one resorts to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *rāja-* to refer to the possessor of the king, it is necessary to maintain that the presence of the meaning of a nominal suffix (*vibhakti-janyopasthiti*) is a cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha-prakāraka-bodha*), in order to exclude the connection of *taṇḍula-* (rice) with the act of cooking through a relation such as objecthood (*karmatva*) in sentences like *taṇḍulaḥ pacati*. [This requirement applies] because the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth do not possess that status [of being the primary meaning of the stem].

In expressions such as "white rice" (*taṇḍulaḥ śubhraḥ*), the rice and so forth are construed with non-difference (*abheda*) precisely within the meaning of the nominative case, which expresses the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, in cases such as "with white rice" (*śubhreṇa taṇḍulena*), the attributive case-ending either signifies non-difference or there is a subsequent (mediated) connection; thus, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. Consequently, since mutual connection between the members of a compound is impossible, the capacity (*śakti*) of the whole for such a qualified meaning is indeed necessary. It is impossible to establish that the compound "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) and the like possess indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, in expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man"), does the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) apply to the related entity (*sambandhin*) or to the relation (*sambandha*)? It cannot be the first, because that would contradict the analysis (*vigraha*) "the man of the king" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), since a sentence that has the same meaning as a compound is alone considered its analysis. Otherwise, the determination of the primary denotative power (*śakti*) could not be established from that analysis. Nor can it be the second, because it would entail the cognition "a man whose nature is the relation to the king," whereas there is a grammatical rule that two nominal stem meanings lacking incompatible case-endings undergo a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*). These points have been elaborated upon in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*.

For this very reason, it is established in the third [book] that in the case of the statement "The first portion belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," it is not proper to enjoin priority with reference to the act of eating, because that would result in the violation of the principle of single-sentence-unity (*ekaprasaratā*). Likewise, in the tenth [book], it is established that in the case of "He sacrifices to Sviṣṭakṛt with three parts," it is not proper to enjoin the number three by way of a restatement of the parts (*aṅga*), because that too would result in the violation of single-sentence-unity. Furthermore, the commencement of the section on the Red Cow (*aruṇādhikaraṇa*) is also consistent [with this view]. If one does not accept a qualified potency (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), there would be the consequence of the section on the Red Cow itself becoming inconsistent.

Otherwise, in the case of the injunction, "One purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed [cow]," just as the word *aruṇā* (ruddy) denotes only the quality of redness, so too the other two words would denote only qualities such as being one year old; since they are immaterial (*amūrta*), their impossibility of serving as instruments for the act of purchasing would be equal [to that of the color]. Consequently, there would be no possibility of suspecting a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) regarding the color alone. This has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. Therefore, the followers of Jaimini must necessarily accept the theory of the expressive power of compounds (*samāsa-śakti-pakṣa*). Let this suffice. || 35 ||

**Determination of the Nature of the Analytic Statement (*vigraha*) in Common Usage and Exposition of the Mīmāṃsaka View:** In expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man"), the analytic statement (*vigraha*) is indeed *rājā cāsau puruṣaśca* ("he who is both a king and a man"). In cases such as *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows"), it is *citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam* ("this one belonging to brindled cows"), because this conforms to the requirement that the compound and its analytic statement must have the same meaning. Although it is understood from the rule *śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.23) that a *bahuvrīhi* compound consists only of words ending in the nominative case, and thus the nominative-ending form [of the analytic statement] is appropriate, the sentence *citragavo yasya* ("he to whom there are brindled cows") is also possible as an alternative formulation.

Because of the rule for compound formation, "The sixth case [is used] when there is a relation" (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.2.8), the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) is, in one view, a sentence. Nevertheless, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that this does not constitute a *vigraha* (analytic expansion), because it has a different meaning; rather, it is only the aforementioned compound itself.
He refutes the Mīmāṃsaka position incidentally:

Whatever has been taught as indicative of the functions of primary and secondary suffixes, a reversal of that [distinction] is observed therein regarding the status of the subordinate and the principal. (36)

It has been stated that the explanatory analysis (*vivaraṇa*) which conveys some portion of the meaning of primary derivatives (*taddhita*) and verbal suffixes (*kṛt*) is called *ākhyāta* (verbal); however, a reversal is observed therein. To illustrate: in the cases of *ākṣikaḥ* ("a gambler") and *kumbhakāraḥ* ("a potter"), the understanding is [respectively] "the locus of an activity having dice as its instrument" and "the locus of an activity conducive to the production of a pot. In the cases of *akṣair dīvyati* ("he plays with dice") and *kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a pot"), the understanding is [respectively] "the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) conducive to gambling, having dice as its instrument" and "the productive urge conducive to the production of a pot."

The point is that even for a Mīmāṃsaka who asserts the primacy of the *kārakas* (grammatical participants) in words formed with *kṛt*-suffixes and the primacy of *bhāvanā* (efficient force) in verbs, a transposition of the aspects of subordinate and principal status does not invalidate the nature of the analysis (*vivaraṇatva*). Thus, there is no obstacle to the phrase "he whose cows are brindled" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) and the like serving as an analysis (*vigraha*) in this context; such is the sense. || 36 ||

Regarding the acceptance of a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), there may be a fear of contradiction with the *Niṣādasthapati-adhikaraṇa*. [Objection: Let it be that, according to the aforementioned method, there is a power in every compound; and let it be that its analysis (*vigraha*) is likewise. Nevertheless, since there is no difference between a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and a *karmadhāraya* in terms of possessing such power, the conclusion established in the *Niṣādasthapati-adhikaraṇa* would not be possible. To this, he says:
"Regarding the acceptance of a distinct power, there is a fear of contradiction with the *Niṣādasthapati-adhikaraṇa*."

The consideration of whether the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*) culminates in resolving the doubt regarding the contradiction with the *Niṣādasthapati* section, which persists in the moments immediately preceding verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). (Verse 37)

And that verbal cognition, being thus finalized, is not far removed from its preceding moment; therefore, by taking up the efficiency (lāghava) existing at that time, there is no contradiction regarding the locus—this is the meaning. The intended sense is as follows: in the view that the compound *niṣādasthapati* possesses a unitary power (*samāsaśakti*), it has multiple meanings because it is simultaneously expressive of: the Niṣāda himself, the chief of the Niṣādas, and another person who is the master of the Niṣādas. Thus, it is polysemous (*nānārtha*) in all these respects.

And thus, according to the maxim "in the case of multiple meanings, comprehension of the specific [meaning] arises from the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*)," when that [intention] is postulated, it is the intention itself that is postulated because of the parsimony [involved] in the fact that both words present only the meaning already previously established; for even for opponents, if there were an intention, the presence of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) would be unavoidable—just as in the case of the command "bring in the staffs"—and therefore intention alone remains as the final candidate for postulation. This is the direction of the argument. || 36 ||
Thus ends the determination of the expressive power of compounds in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra. || 5 ||
Now follows the determination of potency (śakti).
Regarding the nature of power (*śakti*), he states its essential form in connection with that very topic: "Just as there is an innate capacity of the senses toward their respective objects,"
The relationship between words and their meanings is beginningless, as is their mutual fitness.

Just as the senses—the eye and so forth—possess an innate capacity (*yogyatā*) toward their respective objects, such as jars and the like, which consists in being the cause of their visual perception and so on, so too for words, the capacity with respect to meanings is precisely their being the cause of their cognition; that alone is what is meant by "power" (*śakti*).
Refutation of the view that convention (*saṅketa*) is the cause of cognition:
Now, it might be argued that power is not an innate cause of cognition, because it is absent in the case of modern names such as "Devadatta."

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even those who do not know the convention (such as parents) would have a cognition of the relation (*anvaya-bodha*); furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) usage. Therefore, it must be stated that the knowledge of convention is also a cause [of verbal comprehension]. And since that [knowledge] is necessary, let that itself be the primary expressive power (*śakti*).

If it is argued that this [convention] belongs to parents and others in the case of modern [names], while it belongs to God (*Īśvara*) in the case of [words like] "cow" and so on—here it is replied: convention is not a cause in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition of meaning even from one whose power has not been grasped.

Nor is it known in its generality, because even if it were known as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, the undesirable consequence would follow that understanding [of the word's meaning] would occur. Nor is the knowledge of it as a convention (*saṅketa*) the cause; for there is a deviation [in the argument], since even among worldly people, Mīmāṃsakas, and others who lack the knowledge of the convention as such regarding words like "cow" (*go*), understanding of the respective meanings arises only when they possess the apprehension that those words produce the cognition of those meanings.

Nor is the cognition of that [word] such [a cause] by virtue of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the capacity to produce the cognition of the object; for, by even greater parsimony (*lāghava*), our position is established through the very fact of its being the producer of the cognition of the object as the cause. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this regard due to the case of a modern Devadatta and others, where understanding arises from the mere knowledge of a convention; because even there, when one grasps the desire—"May this word convey this meaning"—there is no deviation, since the capacity of that word to convey that meaning is apprehended within the word itself.

Nor should it be asserted that the cognition of a word’s capacity to convey meaning independently is the cause [of understanding]. For otherwise, one who possesses the cognition "this is not the generator of that [specific] cognition" would—while knowing "this meaning was understood by this person from this word"—be subject to the undesirable consequence of grasping that [meaning] as well. This is because for one who possesses the cognition "this is not the generator of that cognition," even if they know the apprehension of another [word] within the word, the grasping of that [meaning] is impossible. Otherwise, even one who knows an error would incur the status of being mistaken themselves.

Furthermore, this capacity to generate the cognition of meaning is grasped only through the knowledge of the convention established by a father or others; therefore, there is no comprehension prior to that knowledge.

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not exist separately, nor does it entail the consequence of the annihilation of that which possesses a primary denotation (*lākṣaṇika*), because this is accepted [by us]; for the linguistic usage that grasps expressive power (*śakti*) is common to both the primary and the indicated meanings. Furthermore, since an apprehension produced by perception and other means is not a constituent factor of verbal cognition, one would have to assert that with respect to verbal cognition, both an apprehension produced by expressive power and an apprehension produced by indication are causes; thus, there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating two distinct causal relations. For us, however, there is parsimony (*lāghava*), as the cause is simply the apprehension produced by expressive power, regardless of its specific nature.

Furthermore, if the occurrence of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) were accepted [as the cause of verbal cognition], there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) for each individual case of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), because verbal cognition arises from an understanding generated by *lakṣaṇā* even without an understanding generated by *śakti* (denotative power). Nor can it be said that the state of possessing those respective understandings—connected by the relation of "immediately preceding"—is the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), while the nature of those respective understandings is the delimiting factor of the cause (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), for that would entail an infinite number of causal relations.

Furthermore, since the cognition of *śakti* (denotative power) and the cognition of *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function) are both causes for the presentation of a word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*), there is a lack of invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāra*). Moreover, the complexity (*gaurava*) should be understood as being exactly as before. The complexity of postulating an infinite number of cause-and-effect relationships is common to all [theories].

Nor should it be argued that even when postulating a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on the knowledge of word-potency (*śakti*) in the form "this word conveys this meaning," the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating multiple causal relations for each distinct meaning is equally yours as well; and that this complexity is even greater if one includes the condition of "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*) to avoid mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For, in accordance with the necessity of accounting for errors regarding potency (*śaktibhrama*), the infinity of causal relations based on the distinction between each specific word and each specific meaning is common to you as well. What remains superior in your view is only the complexity of postulating the causal relations for secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
Even regarding the causality of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) with respect to a presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), there is complexity (*gaurava*).

If it is argued that one should instead maintain that the causality of verbal cognition resides solely in being a presentation produced by a linguistic function, while the causality for the presentation of a word-meaning resides in the knowledge of the linguistic function itself—this is not so. This is because the nature of the linguistic function (*vṛttitva*)—defined either as being either denotative power (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or as a relation between a word and its meaning conducive to a presentation of the meaning that serves as the cause of verbal cognition—is a heavier property than denotative power (*śaktitva*) when it serves as the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). This is because [the latter] would require the knowledge of the linguistic function that causes the presentation of the meaning which delimits the causality of verbal cognition.
Since even the apprehension of the causal relation constituted by that [relation] is impossible,
it is also inconsistent for the cognition of power to be the cause of the definition of power itself.

If it is argued that for me as well, the causality [of word-meaning cognition] resides solely in the knowledge of the capacity (*śakti*), because even in *lakṣaṇā*—which consists in the knowledge of a relation to that which is capable [of denoting the secondary meaning]—the capacity itself is included; we say no. This is because, in the causal relation between the knowledge of capacity and the mental presentation of the object (*padārthopasthiti*), it is necessary that they have the same object (*samānaviṣayatva*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even for one who does not grasp the relation between the Ganges and its bank, but knows the capacity of the word "Ganges," the cognition of the bank would arise from the sentence "There is a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), since the cause—the knowledge of capacity—is present.

Furthermore, consider the sentence "Bring the jar" (ghaṭam ānaya) for one who remembers both a jar and an elephant. For such a person, who possesses a collective recollection (*samūhālambana-smaraṇa*) of the jar and so forth from the word "jar" and of the elephant-driver from the word "elephant," there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding the elephant-driver as well, just as there is one regarding the bringing of the jar. This is because the requirement that the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*)—which takes the form of a collective recollection—is produced by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*, i.e., *pada*) is satisfied in this case.

Consequently, it must be stated that "with respect to a verbal cognition, the cause is a presentation produced by a function directed toward that specific part [of the meaning] as its object. And thus, it is impossible to argue that even *lakṣaṇā* (indication) functions as a cause by virtue of being a knowledge of power (*śakti*).

By this, the following view is refuted: that "the cause [of understanding] is simply a presentation (upasthiti) brought about by the capacity [of the word]," and thus for me as well there is no distinct causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) regarding the knowledge of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for it has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa* that it is difficult to state a definition of "being brought about" (*prayojyatva*) that is not over-extensive (*anatiprasakta*). || 37 ||

Regarding the proof of expressive power (*śakti*) in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*): Now, one might object that since understanding is observed to arise from vernacular speech and the like, expressive power—consisting in the capacity to convey meaning—must also exist there; and consequently, they would also possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*), because it was established in the section on Grammar (*Vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*) that correctness consists precisely in being endowed with expressive power. He resolves this doubt in two ways:
first, by establishing the view that "understanding arises from the recollection of the correct form."
Some maintain that an incorrect word is expressive by means of inference;
or, even if there is no difference in their expressiveness, there is a restriction regarding merit and demerit. (38)

The non-standard forms such as *gāvī* and the like are held by some to be expressive—that is, conveyors of meaning—by means of inference; that is, having inferred the standard word (*sādhuśabda*) through inference, they are considered to be the signifiers. Thus, their utility is merely in the recollection of the standard form, just as in the case of written characters, and not in being direct signifiers of it; therefore, they do not possess the quality of being standard (*sādhutva*). For it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"They are the causes for the arising of cognition regarding the standard forms through inference;
they reveal the word-meaning as if they themselves had attained identity with it."
They are not followed by the learned, just as synonyms are not followed by the virtuous; because they are not sanctioned by the Smṛti scriptures, they are therefore not directly expressive.
When a child being instructed utters "bambabēti," that which is indistinct to him becomes a clear determination for those who know it.
"Thus, when a correct word ought to be employed, if an incorrect form (apabhraṃśa) is used instead, some meaning is expressed by it only through the mediation of that correct word."
Regarding the evidence for the fact that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) do not directly denote meaning:

if it is asked, "What is the proof that corrupt forms do not directly denote meaning, since the grounds for postulating a denotative power (*śakti*), such as linguistic usage, are equal [to those of correct forms]?"—the answer is: true, but because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a denotative power for each of those various forms which differ according to their respective regions. Nor should one suspect they are synonyms, for they are uniform across all regions; thus, in the absence of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-viraha*), the postulation of power applies to all of them. This is not the case with corrupt forms; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of counting different vernaculars as mere synonyms.

And thus, the view of the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others—that "fitness alone constitutes correctness" (sādhutva)—should be understood according to their own tenets. This establishes that even in corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa) there is expressive power (śakti), thereby setting forth our own position.

Now he states his own view: "Or, because there is no difference in their being denoters (*vācakatva*). The underlying idea is this: if corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) were devoid of expressive power (*aśaktatva*), then comprehension would not arise from them at all. Nor can it be argued that comprehension arises from them through the recollection of the corresponding correct word (*sādhu-smaraṇa*), for even commoners who are ignorant of such correct words still achieve comprehension, whereas those [correct words] are not understood by them. Nor can it be argued that comprehension arises from them due to an error regarding expressive power (*śakti-bhrama*), because since the capacity to produce comprehension is uncontradicted, the apprehension of that capacity cannot be an error.

Even under the view that "expressive power is the will of God" (*īśvarecchā śaktiḥ*), there is no contradiction in that [will] which has all existing things as its object; furthermore, since expressive power consists of specific words and meanings, an error regarding it is impossible.
And it is said in the Vākyapadīya:
"When corrupt forms have attained common usage through tradition among speakers who lack proficiency,
for those [forms], the correct word is non-expressive."
"This divine speech has been thrown into confusion by incompetent speakers; however, regarding this doctrine, there is a perversion of intellect among those who perceive only the impermanent."

"Non-denotative" means non-cognitive; "cognitive error" (buddhiviparyaya) means the erroneous notion that "only these [Sanskrit words] are denotative, and no others. Furthermore, due to the absence of any decisive evidence (vinigamanāviraha), there is also expressive power (śakti) in the vernaculars. Nor is their multiplicity a defect, because—just as with Sanskrit—the Marathi and other vernaculars are uniform everywhere, such that the absence of any decisive evidence remains the same for each one.

Furthermore, it must be considered by the wise: while word-order serves to delimit meaning, that order varies from one instance to another even within the vernacular (bhāṣā) just as it does among synonyms; what, then, is the distinction between the two? Thus, since the vernacular is uniform everywhere just like Sanskrit, each individual word is indeed expressive. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of counting the vernaculars as mere synonyms, for it is only the correct forms (sādhūni) that are categorized and defined in lexicons and other works.
As for corrupt forms (apabhraṃśas), although they possess denotative power, they are nevertheless declared to be incorrect.

[Objection: But in that case, would not those [corrupt forms] also possess correctness? To this, he says: "The restriction. There is an injunction for correct words, "One should speak with correct words," intended to teach the production of merit; and there is a prohibition, "Not with incorrect words," intended to teach the production of demerit. Thus, correctness (*sādhutva*) consists in being fit for the production of merit, while incorrectness (*asādhutva*) consists in being fit for the production of demerit. In this regard, correctness is a universal (*jāti*) that delimits the capacity to produce [merit]. And the indicators of that [correctness] are the lexicons (*kośa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth.

In the same way, just as the Rājasūya sacrifice and others do not produce their results when performed by a Brāhmaṇa, it follows that words such as *go* (cow) and so forth do not possess correctness (*sādhutva*) when applied to horses and the like.
Correctness consists in being derived through grammar;

even modern names such as Devadatta possess correctness because they are derived [as valid] by the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "two syllables. Thus, the conclusion is reached that whatever word is derived for a particular meaning in grammar is correct in that sense.

Since secondary (gauṇa) words are derived based on their qualities (guṇa), they possess grammatical correctness (sādhutva) precisely when they function by placing that quality to the fore. However, it is accepted that modern metaphorical (lākṣaṇika) expressions are indeed incorrect. For this very reason, it has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa* that an expression such as "give to the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇaṃ dehi*)—used in the sense of "give to the Brāhmaṇa's [son]" (*brāhmaṇāya dehi*)—is not correct even through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). 38.

The means of apprehending an additional power (atiriktaśakti): he states the means of apprehending an additional power—In the case of a word denoting a relation, the relation [is the basis for] fitness; [and] fitness [is the basis for] fitness.
From convention arises the cognition of fitness, like the relationship between mother, son, and so forth. || 39 ||

The relation is the object. With respect to fitness, fitness is the object; with respect to the word denoting the related, fitness is the object. From convention—that is, from linguistic usage—the cognition of fitness, which is the apprehension of the expressive power (śakti), occurs. The meaning is that through usage—such as "the word 'jar' here is fit for this [object], it is related to this"—that [fitness] is to be grasped. || 39 ||
Thus ends the determination of expressive power (*śakti*) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*. (6)

Now follows the determination of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Superimposition (*āropitatva*) is what is manifested by the negative particle; he states the meaning of the negative particle as follows:
And in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), because the subsequent member is predominant, it possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*).
The state of being superimposed (āropitatva) is what is expressed by the negative particle (nañ), for this [negation] does not go beyond [the meaning of] "not-all" (atisarvavat).

The remainder [of the argument] is that because the subsequent member (uttarapada) is predominant in a negative compound (nañ-samāsa), its status as a pronoun (sarvanāmatā) is established. For this very reason, it must be accepted—as the remainder implies—that "the state of being superimposed" (āropitatva) alone is what is expressed by the negative particle (nañ).

The intended meaning is as follows: in expressions such as *asarvaḥ* ("not-all"), the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) is established because the word *sarva* retains its predominance in the sense "superimposed all. Otherwise, that status would not obtain here, just as it does not in *atisarvaḥ*, since in cases such as *ghaṭo nāsti* ("the pot does not exist"), we observe that the word functions solely as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in a cognition whose object is negation. And according to our view, that resulting cognition is mental (*mānasa*).

And thus, there is no contingency of the non-establishment of forms such as *asarvasmai* and so on. Here, "superimposedness" (*āropitatvam*) means being the object of superimposition (*āropaviṣayatvam*). The essential point is that the meaning is merely the superimposition itself, while "objecthood" (*viṣayatvam*) is the relation (*saṃsarga*). The statement regarding "being expressed" (*dyotyatva*) is made with the intention that particles (*nipātānām*) possess the function of indication (*dyotakatvam*). || 40 ||

Regarding the alternative position that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is non-existence (*abhāva*), he states another view: "Or rather, let non-existence be its meaning, for such is the intention of the Bhāṣya; [this is so] because the cognition of superimposition (*āropa*) in cases such as 'the jar does not exist' or 'a non-Brahmin' contradicts universal experience."
Whether it be the qualifier or the qualified, let it be determined according to the logical rule. || 41 ||

The phrase *tadarthaḥ* (meaning "that is its meaning") refers to the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). The word *artha* is mentioned so as to apply commonly to both the view that [the negation] is indicated (*dyotya*) and the view that it is denoted (*vācya*). Regarding the position that the meaning of the negative particle is non-existence (*abhāva*), there is the authority of the *Bhāṣya*. As for the *Bhāṣya*, it says: "Thus, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Nañ-sūtra*: 'That whose referent has ceased' (*nivṛttapadārthakaḥ*). Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of "that whose referent (*padārtha*) has ceased," according to Pāṇini’s rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (3.3.114). The meaning is "having non-existence as its referent."

As for Kaiyaṭa’s statement that the meaning is "that in which a word-meaning has ceased," or "that whose referents are Kṣatriyas and so forth upon whom Brāhmaṇahood has been superimposed through similarity and the like"—that is not correct, because a Kṣatriya or similar person upon whom Brāhmaṇahood has been superimposed is not the denotation of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Otherwise, similarity and the like would also have to be considered denotations [of *nañ*].
This is a demonstration that similarity and the like are not the meanings of *nañ*.
As for that which is stated:
"Similarity, absence, difference from it, its smallness,
lack of excellence, and opposition— these six are proclaimed as the meanings of the negative particle (nañ)."

Having recited thus, they cite examples such as *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (a non-Brahmin), *apāpam* (sinless), *anaśvaḥ* (not a horse), *anudarā kanyā* (a girl with no belly), *apaśavo vā anye go'śvebhyaḥ* (others are indeed like non-animals compared to cows and horses), and *adharmaḥ* (unrighteousness). It is clear from other sources that this is intended in the sense of the actual reality (*tattvārthika*). Regarding the term "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇam*), the word "counter-correlative" (*pratiyogin*) is to be supplied. Thus, in the case of the word *asarva*, it possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*). [As in the rules] *anekam anyapadārthe* ("many [words] in the sense of another word") and *sevyate 'nekayā* ("is served by many").

In expressions such as *sannatāpāṅgayā* ("by her with downcast eyes"), the rule for the singular number is established because the meaning of the single word [the compound] is predominant. In cases such as *abrāhmaṇaḥ* ("a non-Brahmin"), it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound because the meaning of the final member is predominant. Furthermore, the systematic arrangement of person (*puruṣa*) and number (*vacana*) is justified in instances such as *atvaṃ bhavasi* ("you are not you") and *anahaṃ bhavāmi* ("I am not I"). Otherwise, just as in "the absence of you" (*tvad-abhāvaḥ*) or "the absence of me" (*mad-abhāvaḥ*), where the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are construed with the element of negation (*abhāva*), there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between *yuṣmad* and the finite verb (*tiṅ*). Consequently, the systematic arrangement of person would not be possible.

In our view, however, because of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) that the action of becoming has a non-different substratum just as [the property of] being the counter-correlative of a difference, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not untenable; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "or the qualificand," the word "counter-correlative" (*pratiyoginī*) is to be supplied. The point is this: even though [the term *asan*] is secondary (*gauṇa*) in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), its designation as a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) is not untenable, due to the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.132: "There is elision of the case-ending *su* after *etad* and *tad*, except when they are part of a negative compound and followed by a consonant. For indeed, the qualification "except when in a negative compound" (*anañ-samāse*) is provided precisely to prevent the elision of *su* in cases such as *asaḥ śivaḥ*. Yet, in that instance, the word *tad* does not possess the status of a pronoun, because it is secondary.

Because by excluding [the case] accompanied by the *akac* suffix in the rule "akoḥ," one obtains the inclusion of only the two types of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) therein; thus, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) "in a compound not preceded by the negative particle *naÑ*" (*anañ-samāse*) can be easily explained.

In rules such as *anekam anyapadārthe*, the singular number is used because it conforms to the gender and number of the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Since the term *sub* (a nominal ending) is carried over from the rule *subāmantrite parāṅgavat svare* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), that substantive must likewise end in the singular. Furthermore, if the word *aneka* were taken in the dual, a *bahuvrīhi* compound of many things would not be established; if taken in the plural, a *bahuvrīhi* of two things would not be established. Therefore, the singular is used to include both cases, being intended either as a genus (*jāti*) or as the default (*autsargika*) form.

In the expression “sevyate 'nekayā” as well, the singular number is used in accordance with the gender of the substantive (*yoṣayā*) and to convey the understanding that the act of serving is performed by each [individual] separately; it is not necessitated by the predominance of the meaning of the final member [of the compound]. For this very reason, expressions such as “patanty aneke jaladher ivormayaḥ” are also easily explained.

In expressions such as *na tvaṃ bhavasi* ("you do not exist"), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sense of *yuṣmad* (the second person pronoun) in something other than that [i.e., in its opposite]. The negative particle (*nañ*) is merely a signifier (*dyotaka*). Thus, because the finite verb (*tiṅ*) is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of *yuṣmad* as modified by the difference, the determination of the person (the second person) is established. The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "the action of becoming has as its locus that which is different from you. Similarly, in *na tvaṃ pacasi* ("you do not cook"), the cognition is the absence of an activity conducive to cooking whose locus is non-different from you. In *ghaṭo nāsti* ("the pot does not exist"), the cognition follows the pattern: the absence of existence whose locus is non-different from the pot. This is because the uncompounded negative particle (*asamasta-nañ*) connects only with the verb.

And that non-existence can be [grasped] in the form of absolute non-existence, mutual non-existence, and so forth, because it is cognized in those respective forms; this has been explained in detail elsewhere. || 41 ||
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*. (7)
Now begins the determination of the meanings of particles (nipāta).

The refutation of the Naiyāyika position that prefixes (*prādi*) are indicators (*dyotaka*) while particles (*cādi*) are denoters (*vācaka*): The view of the Naiyāyikas—that prefixes such as *pra-* and so on are indicators, whereas particles such as *ca-* and so on are denoters—is untenable because there is no justification for such a disparity. Suggesting this, he establishes the indicative nature of particles: "By which [reason] prefixes such as *pra-* are indicators, particles such as *ca-* are likewise [indicators]."
Just as the letter *la* is seen [in the word] "hariharau upāsyete" (Hari and Hara are to be worshipped). 42.

By the same reason that particles beginning with *pra* are indicators (*dyotaka*), for that very reason particles beginning with *ca*—the *nipātas*—are likewise indicators; this is the meaning. The underlying point is this: in expressions such as "he experiences the Lord" (*īśvaramanubhavati*), the [action of] experiencing and so forth, which is being perceived, is not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because otherwise it would follow that even in the case of "it exists" (*bhavati*), [the existence] would have to be the meaning of the root.

It does not have the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*) itself; for if that were the case, since it would not be the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), there would be the consequence of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) being unable to connect with its own meaning therein, given the established rule that suffixes convey meanings based on their connection with the meaning of the root. Furthermore, in cases such as *anugacchati* ("he follows"), it would lead to the unintended application of suffixes like the past participle (e.g., *anubhūta*). Nor does it denote a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*), because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, let the verbal root itself—which expresses existence and so forth—be the denoter (*vācaka*), and let the prefix be the indicator of the speaker's intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Thus, being an indicator of intention is precisely what constitutes "suggestiveness" (*dyotakatva*).

And this [objection] applies equally even to cases beginning with *ca* (the particle "and"). For in examples such as "he sees like Caitra," it is easy to say that the word *caitra* denotes by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) Caitra qualified by similarity, while the word *iva* serves to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*). To this, he himself states another argument: "Hari and Hara are worshipped. For here, is the act of worship (*upāsanā*) the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*), of the [word] as a whole, or of the verbal root alone?

Not the first [alternative], because if that were the case, since the root *as* (to be) does not denote a result in the form of meditation—which would require the verb to express an operation whose locus is distinct from its own result—the suffix *lakāra* (the verbal ending) could not occur in the sense of the object (*karman*). Not the second, because of its complexity (*gaurava*). As for the third, the status of being a *dyotaka* (indicator) is attained, since it acquires the function of making the intended meaning (*tātparya*) known; this is the underlying point. In the phrase "it is seen" (*dṛśyate*), the word "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. || 4 ||
He states that the principle— that particles such as *ca* also function merely as indicators—
is equally applicable here:
"Likewise, in other instances, even when used as a particle (*nipāta*), the suffix *la* denotes the object."
The application of two qualifiers is also the same as in the case of *prādi* [prepositions] and so forth, when applied to [words] beginning with *ca*. (43)

This is the case elsewhere, as in examples such as "Śiva is *sākṣātkriyate* (realized), *alaṅkriyate* (adorned), or *ūrīkriyate* (accepted). Here too, in order to establish the *l*-suffix in the object (*karman*) for those respective meanings of the verbal root (*dhātu*), it must be stated that these [prefixes] denote those specific meanings; thus, the meaning is that these, like prefixes (*upasarga*), are denoters (*dyotaka*). Although the root *kṛ* is indeed transitive (*sakarmaka*), nevertheless, in these specific senses, its transitivity would not apply. Otherwise, the sense is that transitivity would also occur in cases such as "the wind *vikurute*" or "the Saindhavas *vikurvate*."

Alternatively, let the meaning of the prefix (nipāta) be the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the object of meditation (*upāsana*) and so forth, in accordance with the natural sense of the lexicon which states, "sākṣāt [is used] in the senses of directness and similarity. Let the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) be the activity conducive to that [realization].

If it is argued that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) can also be easily defined as "possessing an operation whose result is the meaning of either the word itself, its own associated particle, or another [word]," and therefore the example and the thing exemplified are inconsistent and thus this [definition] is not a proof—[we reply: no, because since there is no direct syntactic connection (*sākṣād-anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root due to their difference, there can likewise be no connection between the meaning of a particle and the meaning of a verbal root. Otherwise, in the case of "The rice cooks" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacati*), it would follow that the rice would be connected to the meaning of the verbal root by way of being the object (*karmatā*).

Furthermore, if prefixes (*prādi*) were denoters (*vācaka*), then just as one says "great excellence" (*bhūyān prakarṣaḥ*) or "what kind of certainty" (*kīdṛśo niścayaḥ*), one would also have to say "great *pra*" (*bhūyān pra*) or "what kind of *niḥ*" (*kīdṛśo niḥ*). In our view, since prefixes are meaningless (*anarthaka*), there is no such connection with them; therefore, they must be indicators (*dyotaka*). With this further proof in mind, he says: "By the qualifier," etc. The point is that the undesirable consequence—that "the beautiful conjunction should be seen" (*śobhanaḥ samuccayo draṣṭavyaḥ*) would result in "the beautiful [conjunction] and [it] should be seen" (*śobhanaśca draṣṭavyaḥ*)—is equally avoidable.

Furthermore, if particles were denotative, there would be no possibility of a distinct syntactic relation (*anvaya*) between the meanings of two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) without the use of the genitive case or others; otherwise, the sentence "the king, the man" (*rājā puruṣaḥ*) would entail the meaning "the man related to the king. With this in mind, he says "etc."—the sense being that, just as one says "the conjunction of the *dhava* and the *khadira* trees," one would have to say "of the *dhava* and of the *khadira*" (*dhavasya ca khadirasya ca*). || 43 ||

Regarding the demonstration that there is no evidence for restricting the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*)—which holds that the cause for the cognition of a difference-based relation between a name and its referent is the presentation [of the terms] by means of contradictory case-endings—the following objection is raised:

"Surely, the causal relationship (where the cognition of a difference-based relation between the meanings of two nominal stems is the effect and the presentation by means of contradictory case-endings is the cause) applies only to cases other than particles (*nipāta*); thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Anticipating this, he says: "A word-meaning never relates to a similar [word-meaning] through a division [of case-endings]."
Examine what evidence there is for restricting the application of the particle *ni* to anything other than its primary sense. 44.

"By the similar" means by that which is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*); "it connects" means it connects through identity (*abheda*), this being the ellipsis. "By the dissimilar" means by that which is not co-referential. The meaning is this: there is no evidence for the assumption that the rule of grammatical derivation regarding the connection of two word-meanings as identical applies only to cases other than particles (*nipāta*), and such an assumption would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). For us, since particles are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), there is no such connection [of identity] at all; thus, this fault does not apply. For this very reason, the Naiyāyikas hold that in expressions such as "the jar does not exist," the word "jar" is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote the counter-positive of that [non-existence]. || 44 ||
Furthermore, if particles (*nipāta*) were denotative, there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in poetry and the like;
thus he states another proof:
"As if wishing to uproot the northerners with his arrows as if they were rays of light, [he drank] the fluids as if they were [the essence of] the earth..."
In such cases, there would be no grammatical coordination (anvaya), and consequently, the case endings (sup) would be heard [as distinct]. || 45 ||

The meaning here is that he intends to uproot the Northerners who are like blood with arrows that are like blood. This construction is only consistent provided that the words "blood" (*asṛj*) and so forth refer to things resembling blood, and the particle *iva* functions as a dyotaka (an indicator). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meanings as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

For instance: in the word *usrair*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, the rays (*usra*) are not the instrument here. Even if that which is similar to the object denoted by *iva* were the instrument, its status as an instrument could not be made known by this [third case ending], because it is not the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, since the word *iva* denotes a non-substantial entity (*asattvārthaka*), a third case ending following it is impossible; or, if it were possible, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being heard [in the utterance]. Moreover, there would be the consequence of the third case ending following the word *usra* being construed [with the verb]. Thus he says: "And of the *sup*s" (*supām ca*). This means: "and the hearing of the *sup*s. By the word "and" (*ca*), the non-construction of the third case ending following the word *usra* is conjoined.

In the phrase "ityādau," the word "etc. (ādi) includes such examples as "vāgarthāviva saṃpṛktau" and "pārvatīparameśvarau vande. In these cases, because speech (*vāk*) and meaning (*artha*), as well as Pārvatī and Parameśvara, lack the status of being objects (*karman*) of the verbal action, the coreferential connection (*ananvaya*) of the accusative case ending following them is precluded; furthermore, the impossibility of understanding the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the meaning of the particle *iva* is also subsumed [by this term].

Furthermore, even if the case-ending of the qualifier has non-difference as its meaning, or if it serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), then, provided that the word *iva* is denotative (*vācaka*), there would still be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). This is because arrows similar to rays (*usra*) cannot be construed as distinct from what is presented by the words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Nor can there be a connection through non-difference due to contradiction; for one should not understand the sense to be "the arrow is non-different from that which is non-different from something similar to rays. || 45 ||
Regarding the doubt that the definition of a *tatpuruṣa* compound would be over-narrow if particles (*nipāta*) are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), and the subsequent resolution:

[Objection] "In your view, in cases such as *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, there would be the consequence of the definition of a *tatpuruṣa* being over-narrow; for since the first member is devoid of meaning, there is an absence of predominance (*prādhānya*) of the meaning of the second member. Furthermore, since a prefix (*upasarga*) lacks meaningfulness, it would not possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and consequently, a case-ending (*vibhakti*) could not follow from it. To this, he says:
"And in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the predominance belongs only to that which is indicated by the other [member]."
Taking up precisely the meaning already illuminated [by the verbal root], the nominal suffixes (*sup*) arise according to their names. (46)

In the case of negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) and others, the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) occurs precisely by taking that which is indicated (*dyotya*). The sense is that, by taking that very meaning, the item possesses meaning (*arthavattva*) and thus attains the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In reality, however, the derivation of the case-ending (*sub*) follows from the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82). Alternatively, its status as a nominal stem may be established by the Vārttika *nipātasyānarthakasya*.
