Or it should be understood that particles (*nipāta*) are included by the particle *ca* in the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46), which has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anukta-samuccaya*) for items not explicitly mentioned.
The Bhaṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas agree with the view that particles (*nipātas*) are indicative (*dyotaka*);
therefore, it is logical that particles are indicative. And it has been stated in the *Akṛtyadhikaraṇa-vārttika*:
"Among the four types of words here, the determination of the meaning of two types [the verb and the noun] is [to be established]."
It is performed because doubt arises [regarding them], but not in the case of prepositions (upasarga) and particles (nipāta).
"For there is no operation whatsoever in those two [word and meaning] regarding the expression of the object;
rather, it is that which illuminates the object for which they stand that is considered the denoter. Thus [it is said].

"By means of a prefix (upasarga), the meaning of a verbal root (dhātu) is forcibly perceived as something else, as in the cases of striking (prahāra), eating (āhāra), gathering (saṃhāra), wandering (vihāra), and avoiding (parihāra). Thus it is said.

In this context, the term "prepositional word" (upasargapada) is indicative of particles (nipāta); it should be understood that the term "verbal root word" (dhātupada) refers to [the root] as occurring within another word. || 46 ||

**The Support of the Position that Particles are Denotative:** Now, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is indeed logical that particles (*nipāta*) themselves possess the denotative power (*vācakatva*) for their respective meanings, since there is no sublation of their capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatā*). Furthermore, following the aforementioned reasoning, one might suggest that in expressions such as *pacati*, let the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone have the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the agent, while the suffixes such as *tiṅ* serve merely to indicate the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-grāhakatva*). Anticipating this objection, he states another position:
"The denotative power of particles [is established] by positive and negative concomitance."
Or rather, it is logical; indeed, that very position held by others is our own. || 47 ||

And thus, the principle that "the cognition of a relation through difference between the meaning of a verbal root and the meaning of a nominal stem is not grammatically established" refers to cases other than particles (*nipāta*). The idea is that, since there is no other way, one must also postulate—despite the lack of evidence—that "there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda*) between the meanings of two co-referential nominal stems. The phrase "but not" (*natu*) means that the distinction between prefixes (*prādi*) and particles (*cādi*) as stated by the Naiyāyikas is not correct.
This constitutes the refutation of the position that among particles, some are merely indicative (*dyotaka*) while others are expressive (*vācaka*).

As for the objection that, since all particles (*nipāta*) are denotative, they could already possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) by the rule *arthavat* itself, rendering the injunction "of a meaningless particle" (*nipātasyānarthakasya*) superfluous; [this is not so].

If all [particles] were merely dyotaka (indicative), then the phrase *anarthakasya* (of that which is meaningless) would be redundant. Consequently, one would have to accept that some are dyotaka while others are vācaka (denotative). This is not so; for if that were the case, there would be no way to prevent the opposite view—that *ca*-type particles are dyotaka while *pra*-type particles are vācaka. Furthermore, it is clear from Kaiyaṭa and other commentators that the composition of the Vārttika was intended to include those particles used solely for filling out the meter (*pādapūraṇa*) which are entirely meaningless, and because that [Vārttika] has been rejected.
Thus, the claim made in the *Samuccaya-adhikaraṇa* that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in the view that they are denotative is refuted.

The plural number in "of others" (*pareṣām*) is for the purpose of including the Mīmāṃsakas. Since the mere word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) does not convey a collection (*samuccaya*), whereas it is conveyed upon hearing the word "and" (*ca*), the word "and" itself is the denoter (*vācaka*) of that [collection], not a mere indicator (*dyotaka*). Furthermore, if it were an indicator, one would have to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) in the other words for that [collection], and also postulate an indicator-power (*dyotakatva-śakti*) in the word "and" and so forth; thus there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). This is indeed established in the *Samuccayādhikaraṇa*, and the sense [of the opponent] is that even this is not tenable.

For instance, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are also useful as indicators of intention (*tātparya*). Since it is accepted that the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) resides only in words such as "jar" when combined, and that particles like "ca" serve as indicators of intention—just as context and so forth does not even necessitate the postulation of two separate powers (*śakti*). For us, since comprehension occurs at the time of grasping the secondary signification, the respective causal relations between those [factors] are necessary; the same applies to the grasping of the primary power (*śakti*). Thus, since there is no other alternative to be postulated in either of these two positions, there is no complexity (*gaurava*); therefore, both are considered valid. For this very reason, it is said: "It is the denoter (*vācaka*) of the particulars, or it may be their indicator (*dyotaka*) because of their possibility."

Thus the *Vākyapadīya* is consistent. Suggesting that a restrictive rule—namely, that according to other philosophical systems (darśana), there is either only denotative power (*vācakatva*) or only indicative power (*dyotakatva*)—is not tenable, he says: "This is indeed our view. (47)
Concluding the refinement regarding the nature of particles (*nipāta*), he says:
"That which is the status of being a particle for others is our established position."
Because capacity is all-pervasive, however, it is held that there must be a delimiting factor. || 48 ||

The status of being a *nipāta* (particle) for others consists in being listed in the group beginning with *ca* while having a meaning that does not denote a sentient being (*asattvārthaka*), as well as possessing the designation "particle" through the relation of denotative power (*śakti*). Whether this is a universal (*jāti*) or an adventitious property (*upādhi*), it is exactly the same for us as well. However, because means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) favor general properties, whether it be denotative power or suggestiveness (*dyotakatā*), it must be postulated as being delimited by that [general property] alone. Thus, the meaning is that the alleged difference between *pra* and *ca* as stated by the Naiyāyikas is untenable; this is because of its pervasiveness—that is, its generality. The mention of "denotative power" (*śaktatā*) is illustrative; it should also be understood to include "suggestiveness" (*dyotakatā*). || 48 ||
Thus ends the determination of the indicative nature (*dyotakatva*) and other functions of particles (*nipāta*) in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*. (8)
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the *tvādi* suffixes and abstract (*bhāva*) suffixes.

Regarding the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) according to the Grammarians' view, he states the meaning of the abstract suffix: "From *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound words, [the meaning of the abstract suffix arises] based on differences of opinion."
The meaning of the suffixes -tva and -tal has been explained by Hari in the commentary. || 49 ||

To dispel the misconception held by the Mīmāṃsakas and others—that there is a Vārttika statement which says, "The expression of a relation [is effected] by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) after primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*), except in cases of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), where the form is non-different [from the base], or where the relation is invariable"—he says, "In the *Ṭīkā*. This means in the *Mahābhāṣya-Ṭīkā* by Bhartṛhari. The phrase "of *tva* and *tal*" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for abstract suffixes in general.

The meaning is this: it has been stated that when power (*śakti*) is postulated in the case of compounds and the like, it is postulated as qualified by the relation with the king and so forth. Thus, the suffix following such [a compound] expresses the relation. Furthermore, since this is not possible under the view of "difference" (*bheda*) among the positions stated—namely, "is it difference, or relation, or both?"—he says "due to the difference of opinion," which means "due to the difference of positions."

And thus, in cases such as *rājapuruṣatva* (the state of being a king’s man), *aupagavatva* (the state of being Upagu’s descendant), and *paktṛtva* (the state of being a cooker), there arises a comprehension of the relation (*anvaya*) consisting respectively of the relation of owner and owned, the relation of parent and offspring (or the relation of offspring and its own offspring), and the relation of action and agent. However, regarding *aupagava* and the like, where the relation is invariable, one should cite as examples secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) that function with a different meaning.

In cases such as "the state of being Dāmodara" or "the state of being a black serpent," because there is a cognition of a specific genus (*jāti*), he says "elsewhere"—meaning: elsewhere than from conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), from non-different forms, and from relations that are invariable. Conventional usage has been explained. An example of the second [type] is "whiteness."

In this context, although the suffix *matup*—governed by Pāṇini’s rule *tadasyāstyasmin* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.14)—is elided by the Vārttika *guṇavacanebhyo matupo lugiṣṭaḥ*, the quality (*guṇa*) itself appears as the qualifier (*prakāra*) because of the cognition of non-difference in such cases as "the jar is white" (*ghaṭaḥ śuklaḥ*), even though the word ends in a *taddhita* suffix. The third [type] is "existence is the state of being" (*sataḥ bhāvaḥ sattā*). Here, the suffix denotes the genus (*jāti*) alone; such is the general direction. || 49 ||
Refutation of the Mīmāṃsaka view:

Regarding those who consider themselves Mīmāṃsakas and assert that in cases such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer"), the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) denotes merely the substance qualified by the meaning of the base noun, [the author] says: "In this matter, there would be the 'half-old-woman' fallacy for those who follow other philosophical systems."
But listen to the two positions established in our own system regarding the primordial principles (tattvas) and so forth. || 50 ||

This concerns the domain of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*). For instance, in cases such as *dāmodaratvam* (the state of being Dāmodara) or *ghaṭatvam* (the state of being a jar), since the abstract suffix does not denote a relation according to the Mīmāṃsakas, it would follow that it could not denote one in cases such as *daṇḍitvam* (the state of possessing a staff) either. Indeed, that which is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*), and which inheres in the meaning of that base, is what is denoted by the abstract suffix following it.

Otherwise, in the case of "ghaṭatvam" (pot-ness), substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like would result in being denoted by the abstract suffix following that term; and in the case of "daṇḍitvam" (staff-bearer-ness) and so on, the staff and the like would likewise result in being denoted by that subsequent abstract suffix. Furthermore, in that system, the relation is not the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition of "daṇḍī" (staff-bearer) and similar terms. As it has been said: "When no other quality inherent in itself exists here as the denotable object, then, due to the absence of any other recourse, the relation is resorted to as the denotable object."

That is not so; for since terms such as *ina* (possessive suffixes) are justified as denoting a relation (*sambandha*), there is no lack of a logical ground [for their application]. This has already been explained in detail at the very beginning of the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*. Now, one might ask: "How is this discrepancy [of yours] also resolved? To this he says: "But in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)... The word "arise" (*jāyante*) is to be construed with the qualifier that will be mentioned later. The meaning is: in the established doctrine, suffixes such as *tvā* arise as the qualifiers (*prakāra*) within the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*). The construction is: two positions are maintained regarding the phrase "the qualifier in the cognition produced by the base. || 50 ||
Regarding the statement "the qualifier in a cognition produced by a base," there are two positions; he states those two positions as follows:
"Resorting to a functional adjunct (prayogopādhi), [one may maintain] that [the meaning of the suffix] is the qualifier of the meaning of the base."
Or rather, it should be stated that these [words] are merely phenomena (dharmas), or else they are subordinate to the word itself.

The suffixes *tvā* and so forth arise when the mode (*prakāra*) produced by that [verbal root]—which is designated as a "state" (*bhāva*)—is the occasioning factor (*upādhi*) in the usage. This occurs by relying on a property (*dharma*) appearing as a mode as being the expressed meaning (*vācyatā*). That is to say, the meaning of *tvā* and so forth is the mode in the cognition produced by the verbal base (*prakṛti*).

Now, one might object: "In the case of *ghaṭatvam* (potness), since *ghaṭatva* is a qualifier (*prakāra*), the suffix expressing the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) following it would imply that *ghaṭatvatva* (the property of being potness) must also be denoted. To this, he states the acceptance of the conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) with the words "mere property" (*dharmamātram*); the intention is that there is no consideration here of whether a term is light or heavy [in its denotation]. This is because the very existence (*sattā*) of Brahman, as qualified by this or that individual instance, takes the form of *ghaṭatva*, *ghaṭatvatva*, and so forth. As it is said: "Existence itself, appearing differentiated among cows and other things due to the difference in their correlates, is called a 'universal' (*jāti*); all words are established in that [existence]."
They declare that to be the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root;
it is eternal, it is the Great Self, and they call it by suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*.

Thus it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*. Furthermore, regarding the rule "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* [are used] after that [word] to express its state" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 5.1.119), the authors of the *Vārttikas* have said: "When a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that quality."

The meaning is that when a word is applied—that is, when its usage occurs—with respect to a substance (*dravya*), which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because of the existence of a quality (*guṇa*) appearing as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), then the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used for that expressed object (*vācya*). Thus, from words such as *rūpa* (form), the suffix occurs with reference to the universal (*jāti*); from words such as *śukla* (white), *aṇu* (minute), *dīrgha* (long), and *mahat* (great), it occurs with reference to a quality (*guṇa*); and from words such as *pācaka* (cook), it occurs with reference to an action (*kriyā*). From words such as *ghaṭa* (pot), the suffix occurs with reference to the universal, because words like *rūpa* generate a cognition in which the universal is the qualifier (*prakāra*). As for words like *pācaka*, since they generate a cognition in which an action is the qualifier, the suffix occurs with reference to that action.

The point is that, according to the view that [a word] generates a cognition whose mode is the relation (*saṃsarga*), the determination of what constitutes "the relation" is easily established. In that case, for words denoting universals (*jāti*), the individuals themselves are the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatā’vacchedaka*). Thus, in the case of the term "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvam*), one should understand that the resulting cognition is: "the unique property residing in pots," and so forth.

He states another alternative: "Or else (*yadvā*). This is based on the statement in the *Vārttika*: "Or else, all things (*bhāvāḥ*) exist by means of their own object (*svenārthena*); that is their 'being' (*bhāvaḥ*). The word "or else" (*yadvā*) also serves the purpose of indicating that [alternative]. They "exist" (*bhavanti*)—that is, they function—as denoters; thus, "things" (*bhāvāḥ*) refers to words. They "exist" or "function" by means of their own form as the object. Therefore, "that is their being" means it is the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*). The point is this: like the object, the word is also a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the substance (*dravya*).

This is because it is universally established that from words such as *hari*, *hara*, *nala*, *ikṣvāku*, *yudhiṣṭhira*, *vasiṣṭha*, and so on, there arises a cognition characterized by the word itself, namely that "there was someone denoted by each of those [names]. Otherwise, [words like] the category of forest herbs (*vanauṣadhivarga*) would fail to convey meaning to city-dwellers. In this very way, the experience regarding words with unestablished meanings is universally established; however, it does not occur through the differentiation of specific universals (*jāti*) and so forth, as is the case with words like *ghaṭa* (pot). Thus, both [the word and the universal] serve as delimiters (*avacchedaka*).
For one who has grasped the linguistic convention (*śaktigraha*) in such a manner, the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) occurs precisely in the form of the universal and so forth.

The apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*), however, does not require [the potency] to be specified by the individual word-form. Rather, it is required only in such forms as "this word has potency toward some [meaning], because it is a correct word" (*sādhupada*). Thus, even from words whose potencies have not been specifically grasped, comprehension occurs in that very same way. And so, it has been explained in detail in the *Bhūṣaṇa* that "the suffix *-tva* also has 'word' (*śabda*) as its meaning. (51)
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the abstract suffixes (bhāvapratyaya) such as *tva* and others, in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra. (9)
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the suffixes denoting deities (*devatāpratyaya*).

The meaning of the suffix in the rule *sāsya devatā* (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.2.24) is that which is to be given (*deya*) as qualified by a deity. In cases such as *aindrī* and *vaiśvadevī*, since there is no other means to bring to mind the status of Indra and others as deities, it is necessary to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the suffix to present them in that specific form. For this very reason, it is said: "This secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) indeed expresses the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) as conjoined with the deity."
"Due to the proximity of the word *āmikṣā*, it is that very [word] which provides the object [for the injunction]. Thus [it is said].

With the intention that even the Mīmāṃsakas have stated: "A taddhita suffix denoting a deity, when occurring after the word 'agni', expresses the deity only when it is used alone; it is not capable of establishing Agni as the deity when joined with another [word]," he says:
The meaning of the base is a qualifier for one part of the meaning of the suffix.
And here, non-difference is the relation; this is the established position regarding the offering to Agni and others.
Whether the potency resides in the deity or in the object to be offered, let it exist as a whole or in parts. (53)

"In a single part" means in the form of the deity. And he says "and non-difference" to show that this qualification [of the deity] occurs through non-difference. Now, one might object with the intention that since the deity is a single part of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), there can be no connection of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) with it even through non-difference; with this in mind, he says "in the deity"—the sense being that, in such a case, there is not even the status of being a single part of a word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśatā*). || 53 ||

The various positions [held by others] are as follows: that the deity is the primary meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) while the object to be given (deya) is the primary meaning of the base (prakṛti); or that there is denotative power (śakti) toward the object to be given and figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) toward the deity, and so forth. Now, one might object: since the deity such as Agni is obtained through the base itself, there is no need to postulate denotative power (śakti) for that [base]. Nor is such power postulated for the sake of bringing about the presentation [of the deity] in its form as a "deity" (devatātva), because such a presentation is possible through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) from the base alone. This is stated with the intention that it is like the cognition of "excellent victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*) in the word *prajayati* according to the theory that prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely illuminators (*dyotaka*). Thus he says:
Either the power (śakti) alone is to be offered, or there may be a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) of the primordial matter (prakṛti);
or it is established as a conventional usage (nirūḍha) referring to the deity—these are all the positions maintained.

Nor should it be argued that since the substance [of the offering] is obtained from another word in cases such as "aindraṃ dadhi" (the curd for Indra), why should the suffix's capacity for that [substance] be postulated? For its cognition occurs even when no other word is heard, and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in "aindraṃ dadhi.

Otherwise, even the verbal suffix would not denote the agent or the object. Furthermore, for the Mīmāṃsakas, let the meaning of the suffix simply be "divinity" (*devatātva*); since the substance is indeed obtained from another word, why can one not say that the suffix should not have denotative power for the substance, just as it does not for the agent in the case of a verbal suffix? This is the general direction of the argument.

The meaning is that the term *devatā* is established (*nirūḍhā*) in its sense as a deity by way of its form; thus, it is not preceded by the cognition of an impossibility (*anupapatti-jñāna*), or rather, its essence (*tattva*) consists in being delimited by beginningless usage.
He states that the determination of the meaning of other secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) elsewhere should also be understood in this same manner.
In the case of [derivatives] such as *krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.58) and *tadasyāsti* (Pāṇini 5.2.94), this same method is traditionally held to apply;
in reality, however, it is simply a matter of linguistic usage (*vṛtti*), so no further effort is made here.

Regarding the rule *tadasyāṃ praharaṇam iti krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.2.57), the meaning here is either a game characterized by a weapon (*praharaṇaviśiṣṭā krīḍā*), or the game and the weapon together (*praharaṇakrīḍe*), or the game alone. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), rules such as *so'sya nivāsaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.3.89), *sā'smin paurṇamāsīti* (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.2.21), and *tadasyāstyasminniti matup* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.14) are included.

Since the capacity [of a word] for something additional is obtained from the rule "A rule concerning words applies when they are semantically capable" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.1.1), the aforementioned investigation was stated in accordance with the method of other systems of thought. Alternatively, it may be said by taking the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) as superimposed. He states "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) to show that the presentation of meaning occurs through a specific capacity alone. || 55 ||
Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the suffixes denoting deities in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra. || 10 ||
Now follows the determination of the number "one" as non-difference.

The presentation of the established doctrine (siddhānta) that the number of non-dual unity (abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā) appears in the state of functional integration (vṛtti); in connection with this discussion of integration, he establishes the doctrine that the number of non-dual unity is perceived therein by means of an illustration:
"It is an established principle (sthiti) that the number of non-dual unity manifests in the state of integration."
Just as, in the statement regarding the sacrifice of kapiñjala birds, the number three is expressed by means of logical reasoning (nyāya). || 56 ||

Regarding this, the first position is that specific numbers exist in an undifferentiated state; that is, the existence of specific numbers in an undifferentiated manner is the number of non-differentiated unity (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*). And it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"Just as all the potencies of medicinal herbs are contained within honey..."
"They exist without distinction; they know that number to be of such a kind. Thus [it is said].

The second position is that it is a generality of number from which particularities have been discarded; or rather, it is that generality of number itself with its particulars abandoned. And it has been said:
"Or, through the abandonment of its distinctions, that essence of number is of such a nature."
Due to the operation of the universal-part, it does not apply when distinctions are excluded.

"Just as one possessing form is perceived through a form whose specific qualities are not grasped—such as white and so forth—but rather the exclusion of differences (bhedāpoha) is what is understood. Thus [it is said].

In this commentary, the remainder is that its manifestation in compounds and the like is established by logical necessity; such is the established position of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*). The underlying point is this: in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man"), an inquiry arises as to whether "this man belongs to the king," "to the two kings," or "to the kings. Since a specific inquiry is preceded by a general cognition, the cognition of that [relation] in a general form must necessarily arise from the word. Therefore, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in that [general relation].

He states the reasoning for its being perceived as singular with the words "kapiñjala" (partridge): the point is that just as, in the counting of a plurality, the number three is the first to be presented [to the mind] and thus appears in that very form, so too singularity is the first to be presented in all cases. The third position—that there is no perception of number at all—is not tenable; in fact, the desire to know [the number] is not established by experience. Or, if it were so, since the relationship of cause and effect between knowledge and desire occurs only when they share the same mode of presentation (*samānaprakāraka*), it should be understood that the denotability [of the word] would likewise be in that very form. || 56 ||
The third position is that there is no cognition of number at all;
thus concludes the determination of the number "one" as non-difference in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*. 11.

Now, the determination of whether number is intended to be expressed or not: following the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*), the intention or non-intention of expressing the number of both the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) is investigated, as this follows from the context of number itself.
Thus, he explains the intention or non-intention of expressing the number of the subject and the predicate.

Since, according to the requirements of the context, it is accepted that number is sometimes primary and sometimes secondary, there is no basis for resorting to reasons such as "the animal being one" [as a restrictive factor]. (57)

Regarding the statement, "He cleanses the cup (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*)," we do not maintain an absolute rule that the qualifiers of the subject (*uddeśya*) are never intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), as one might think from that example. This is because, in the rule *dhātoḥ* ("after a verbal root"), the singular number is indeed intended to be significant; for if the suffix were to arise after all verbal roots [simultaneously], then it would be qualified by all of them, just like the case-ending (*subartha*) produced after a *dvandva* compound. Thus it is said: "If the suffix were to arise after all verbal roots, then it would be qualified by all of them, just like the meaning of the case-ending produced after a *dvandva*."

Furthermore, this is because Bhaṭṭapāda states so in the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*, and because in the rule "ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.35), the quality of being "valādi" (beginning with a consonant) is intended as a qualifier of the *ārddhadhātuka* which is the subject of the injunction (*anuvādya*).

Likewise, there is no fixed rule that a qualifier of an injunction must be intended [as significant], just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), for otherwise, in the rule "radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ" (8.2.42), the prescription of two *na*s would not be possible; consequently, the occurrence of two *na*s in the form "bhinnaḥ" would not take place. [This is also supported by] "ād guṇaḥ" [1.1.2].

The sense is that since the [grammatical] justification for examples such as [Pāṇini 6.1.87] is possible by intending only singularity (*ekatva-vivakṣayā*), the mention of the word "one" (*eka*) in [Pāṇini 6.1.84], "one [substitute occurs] in place of both the preceding and the following," would otherwise result in being redundant. As for the meaning of the words: since, in accordance with the observed instances (*lakṣya-anurodhāt*), it is accepted that number is sometimes primary (*tantra*) and sometimes secondary (*atantra*), therefore the recourse to the reasons stated in the section on the singularity of the animal (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*) is not established in our own system (*siddhānta*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatva*) is included. || 57 ||
Regarding the number of the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*), there is sometimes an intention to express it (*vivakṣā*) and sometimes no such intention.

Now, it must be argued that the expression of the qualifier of the *vidheya* is necessary; otherwise, in cases such as *sudhyupāsyaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of *y* sounds, and in *bhinnaḥ*, there would be the consequence of other [nasals] as well, just like the two *n* sounds. Furthermore, the mention of "one" (*eka*) in the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is intended to prevent a difference in the substitute (*ādeśa*) due to a difference in the original bases (*sthānin*). With this in mind, he says: "In the case of the *vidheya*, a differentiator is essential; there is no restriction from elsewhere."
The reliance upon reasons such as the oneness of the cup (grahaikatva) and so forth is without foundation. 58.

The term *bhedaka* means a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). The term *tantra* means "intended" (*vivakṣita*). Let it be granted that the qualifier of the predicate (*vidheya*) is intended; nevertheless, there is no restriction regarding the subject (*anuvādya*) from another source. The meaning is that in some cases it is intended (*tantra*), while in others it is not. As for the reason [given] in the case of the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatva*) and so forth—namely, the non-difference of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and so on—the resorting to that here is without foundation. The sense is that it is possible to enjoin the augment *iṭ* and so forth by taking as the basis (the *uddeśya*) a verbal root qualified by singularity, and an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix qualified by having *valādi* (beginning with consonants other than *y*) as its cause. || 58 ||
Regarding the justification for obtaining two *n* sounds in the rule *radābhyām*:
one might object that, if this were the case, two *n* sounds would not be obtained in the word *bhinnaḥ*; therefore, he says:
"Because two *n* sounds are obtained through a division of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) in the rule *radābhyām*."
There is no deficiency in the status of being a tantra, for the distinction lies in that which is to be enjoined. || 59 ||

The meaning is that by adopting two distinct syntactical constructions—namely, "the *na* of the *niṣṭhā*" [suffix] indicated by the particle *ca*, and "the *na* of the preceding *da*"—the attainment of two *na*s is achieved. || 59 ||
Thus ends the determination regarding the intentionality of number in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra. 12.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the suffixes *ktvā* and others.
The meaning of the base (prakṛti) in the case of indeclinable kṛt-affixes is indeed the abstract state (bhāva); he now defines the meaning of the suffix *ktavatu* and others:
"Because of the statement 'indeclinable kṛts,' the suffixes *tumun* and so forth [express] the meaning of the base."
It is established that for these [suffixes], the identity of the agent and so forth is what is indicated (dyotya). || 60 ||
“*tumādayaḥ*” means *tumun*-affixes and so forth. “In the sense of the base (*prakṛtyarthe*)” means in the sense of the action (*bhāve*).

By the word “and so forth” (*ādinā*), the inclusion of the *ktavatu* affix and others is intended. He states the authority for the rule “in the sense of the action” (*bhāve*) with the words “*avyayakṛta iti*”; the meaning is that this is based on the Vārttika: “*avyayakṛto bhāve*” (the indeclinable kṛt-affixes denote the action). Now, one might ask: what is the status of rules such as “*samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*” (when two actions have the same agent, the suffix is used for the earlier time)? To this he replies: “*samānakartṛkatvādīti*. The point is this: in examples such as “*bhoktuṃ pacati*” (he cooks in order to eat) and “*bhuktavā vrajati*” (having eaten, he goes), the fact that they form a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*) is universally established; yet this would be untenable without a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the actions of eating and cooking.

Otherwise, even in cases such as "he eats" (*bhuṅkte*) and "he goes" (*vrajati*), there would result the undesirable consequence of their being a single sentence. Thus, the relation that determines the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between those two is manifold, including: the relation [of action], the state of being produced (*janyatva*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the relation of preceding and succeeding [moments], pervasion (*vyāpyatva*), and so forth. Accordingly, in instances such as "he cooks in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pacati*) and "having eaten, he is satiated" (*bhuktvā tṛptaḥ*), the cognition is: "the act of cooking is the producer of eating," and "satiation is produced by eating."

For this very reason, even though satisfaction exists after drinking water, the expression "having drunk, [he is] satisfied" (*pītvā tṛptaḥ*) is not employed. Since coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also a relation, coreferentiality by the same agent is obtained by implication. In cases such as "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktavā vrajati*), the relation consists of both temporal sequence (*pūrvottarabhāva*) and coreferentiality; thus, the understanding is that the action of going occurs at a time subsequent to and is coreferential with the action of eating.

In expressions such as "he stands having studied" (*adhītya tiṣṭhati*) or "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*), [the gerund suffix] is not used at times when the acts of studying or opening the mouth are absent; rather, whenever his standing or sleeping occurs, there is [simultaneously] studying or opening the mouth. Thus, there is a cognition of pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) delimited by specific times. Pervasion and co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) constitute the relation (*saṃsarga*).
Properties such as having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) are not directly expressed [by the suffix].

And thus, since they are obtainable elsewhere, it is not correct to conclude from the Sūtra that they possess the status of being denotative (*vācyatva*); this is established by the rule "the indeclinable *kṛt*-suffixes denote the action" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*). Consequently, the suffixes such as *ktvā* function as indicators (*dyotaka*) whose nature consists in conveying the intention regarding the connection between the meaning of the verbal root and the action. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa, taking up the portion of the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra "samānakartṛkayoḥ" which states "because it is expressed by its own word, [it is] not [denoted]," explains: "The sense is that *ktvā* and the like are prescribed when the time of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) is to be indicated, but not when that [time] is the object [of denotation].
This raises the doubt that the status of being denotative is necessary for [properties] such as having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).

As for the claim that "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) is expressed by the suffix *-ktvā* based on the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ*, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sentence "Having cooked the rice, I shall eat" (*odanaṃ paktvāhaṃ bhokṣye*), because [the agent] is not expressed; nor can it be argued that the instrumental does not arise because the agent is denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*), for even though the agent of the act of eating is denoted, the agent of the act of cooking is not.

This is because the rule "anabhihite" (when not already expressed) is understood as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). For this very reason, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that in the example "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*), although the substratum of the action of ascending (*prasādana*) is expressed, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) occurs because the substratum of the action of sitting (*āsti*) is not expressed. Therefore, the doubt—that the expression of the agent by the *ktvā* suffix is necessary, and consequently the expression of shared agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) and so forth must also be necessary—is refuted.

That is not so, because that meaning cannot be obtained from the sūtra; for its meaning is simply: "The suffix *ktvā* is used when two actions have the same agent, [the action] occurring at the earlier time. Otherwise, the formulation of the sūtra would have been merely "when there is a common agent" (*samānakarttari*). As for the introduction of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*), it is impossible, because the agent of the primary action denoted by the finite verb is already expressed, and grammatical operations apply to the subordinate element in accordance with the principal one. And it has been said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"Where there are two distinct powers belonging to a substance in respect to a primary and a secondary action, and those powers reside in subordinate factors, there the principal factor prevails."

"The power whose primary object [is the agent] is expressed by the suffix; when [the action] is a subordinate factor (guṇa), then it is understood even though not explicitly stated. Furthermore, otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the object (*karman*) would also be the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā*, because in the sentence "Having cooked, rice is eaten by me," the accusative case-ending could not be prevented by any other means. Let this suffice for the detailed discussion. || 60 ||
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* and others in the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra. || 12 ||
Now begins the examination of the sphoṭa.
The established conclusion is that the sentence-sphoṭa alone possesses primacy; he states the final determination of this conclusion:
"The position of our school is that the sentence-sphoṭa remains as the ultimate refinement."

Although there are eight positions established as the final doctrine—namely, the letter-sphoṭa (varṇasphoṭa), the word-sphoṭa (padasphoṭa), the sentence-sphoṭa (vākyasphoṭa), the indivisible word-sphoṭa and sentence-sphoṭa, and three universal-sphoṭas (jātisphoṭas) distinguished by letter, word, and sentence—the inclusion of the term "sentence" (vākya) would otherwise be redundant or even meaningless; nevertheless, it is included to demonstrate that all others besides the sentence-sphoṭa are likewise unreal. This very point is emphasized by the phrase "in the ultimate analysis. Such is the settled view of the Grammarians, beginning with the author of the Mahābhāṣya. This concludes the exposition of the letter-sphoṭa.

Therein, examining all of them in sequence, he first states the *varṇasphoṭa*: "The word *sādhu*..."—the point of contention is whether the expressive [units] are contained within the correct (*sādhu*) words or not.
[The author's position is: The expressive [units] are contained within the correct words, but they are not [directly] remembered by them. (61)

The first alternative belongs to others; "no," say the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*). When a correct word such as *pacati* ("he cooks") or *rāmaḥ* ("Rāma") is employed, it is precisely the internal *asti*, the visarga, and so forth, that are the conveyers—that is, the denoters—because it has been previously established that only those possess the capacity for denotation (*śaktatva*). The meaning is that it is not the *la*-affixes or *sva*-affixes remembered [from their original forms] by those [internal elements] that are the denoters. (61) This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that those elements situated within the actual usage do not possess denotative power.

However, those elements such as *asti*, *visarga*, and so forth that are included within the grammatical application (*prayoga*) are not denotative; for if they were, their multiplicity would result in an infinite number of expressive powers (*śakti*). Furthermore, in cases such as *edhāñcakre* and *brahma*, it is impossible for substitutes (*ādeśa*) or elisions (*luk*), which are of the nature of absences, to possess denotative capacity. Rather, the *lakāra*s (tense markers) and suffixes such as *su* and others, which are recalled by these [elements], are the denotators. This is because *latva* (the property of being a *la*-marker), being a universal (*jāti*), is appropriately suited to be the delimiting factor of the expressive power (*śaktatā’vacchedaka*), and because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*). The substitutes, on the other hand, are diverse and mutually deviant.

And because this is in accordance with grammatical rules such as "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69). For they say that we do not find any grammatical rule indicating that substitutes (ādeśa) possess denotative power.

He refutes those [opponents] who attempt to establish the denotative capacity of elements occurring within actual usage by means of their own supporting arguments: [The following passage follows: ... he refutes them with his own supporting arguments—

Furthermore, because of its established status, its conventional usage, and the logic of its being the cause [of that usage], if it were the case that the present tense (*laṭ*) alone was merely being reminded by the verbal suffixes such as *śatṛ* and others; 62.

Consider how the agent (kartṛ) may be either inexpressible or expressible; this distinction follows from the established rule that only those elements included within the actual linguistic usage are denotative, and not those merely recalled by them. For instance, in cases such as *pacati*, for one who does not know the *lakāra* suffix...

It does not denote that [meaning] because it is understood from the [original] base (*ādeśin*). Nor is the understanding of those [substitutes] due to an error regarding their expressive power (*śakti*), for there is no evidence that such an understanding is erroneous; furthermore, since various grammarians arbitrarily accept different original bases (*ādeśins*), there would be no settled rule as to which one possesses the expressive power and which does not. If all were considered expressive, there would be both unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*). Since the substitutes (*ādeśas*) are fixed by virtue of being included within actual usage, it is appropriate that they possess the expressive power. Thus, there is the parsimony (*lāghava*) of not having to postulate the recollection of the original bases.

He states another argument for proof: "Because of linguistic usage" (*vyavahṛteḥ*). Linguistic usage is indeed the primary means among those that grasp word-potency (*śakti*). And since that usage occurs only with respect to the *tiṅ* suffixes and the like as they are actually heard, the meaning is that these alone are the expressive agents (*vācaka*). Furthermore, regarding the principle of "the cause of that" (*taddhetunyāya*): if the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) were the conveyor of meaning, then comprehension would arise even from the form "bhū l". If it is argued that in such a comprehension, the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "bhavati" is also a cause, then, because it is indispensable, let the power of expressiveness belong to that very co-occurrence itself.

Otherwise, there would be the complexity of postulating both that the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) possesses denotative power and that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) [of the letters] is the cause [of meaning]. Thus, since there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) to prefer the view that "it is such letters in co-occurrence [that denote]" over the other, the conclusion is reached that the letters contained within the actual usage are the denoters; this is the intended sense.

Furthermore, if only the *la*-suffix were the expressive element (*vācaka*), the established distinction in your own doctrine—that the *kṛt* suffixes express the agent (*kartṛ*) and the *tiṅ* suffixes express the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—would not hold true; thus he says "moreover" (*kiñca*). The sense is that if the substitutes (*ādeśa*) themselves were the expressive elements, then it would be logically consistent to maintain the distinction that the power (*śakti*) to express productive activity resides in the *tiṅ* suffixes, while the power to express the agent resides in [suffixes] such as *śānac*.

Nor should it be suspected that, although the action (*kṛti*) is not the meaning of the *l*-suffixes [in general], let the locus (*āśraya*) be the meaning of the *śānac* suffix and so on, because of the grammatical rule "the *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). For that rule does not apply to the *śānac* suffix and others, as they are already satisfied by the meaning of their substituends (*sthānin*). Otherwise, it would apply even to the *ghañ* suffix and others. || 62 ||

The refutation of the doubt that the suffix *śānac* denotes the agent because of the requirement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): Having raised the objection that the agent must be the expressed meaning of *śānac* due to the requirement of coreferentiality in examples such as "Devadatta, while cooking" (*devadattaḥ pacamānaḥ*), he says:
"In forms ending in *-tarap* and so on, as well as in finite verbal forms (*tiṅ*), the status of being a noun (*nāmatā*) exists clearly, just as it does in *kṛt* suffixes. (63)

Therefore, let it be understood that the non-difference between the name (the word) and its meaning is likewise established. The point is this: in expressions such as "Maitra cooks better" (*pacatitarāṃ maitraḥ*) and "Maitra cooks somewhat" (*pacatikalpaṃ maitraḥ*), since the identity and the relation of coreferentiality (*abhedānvaya*) are possible because [the suffix] denotes the meaning of the noun, the suffix must be a denoter of the agent (*kartṛvācakatā*). Nor can it be argued that in "pacatikalpam," there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward the agent in order to maintain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for if that were so, the same would apply to the form "pacamānaḥ" (the present middle participle). Furthermore, the grammatical rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) is explained by taking the denotation of the agent and so forth to be attributed to the suffix *l*, which is postulated on the basis of parsimony (*lāghava*). || 63 ||
Thus concludes the examination of the phoneme-sphoṭa.
The Definition of *Padasphoṭa*: The Definition of *Sakhaṇḍapadasphoṭa* (the definition of *padasphoṭa* as a technical term, namely that "a word is that which possesses expressive power").
Now, if substitutes (*ādeśa*) are the denoters, then the *padasphoṭa* is clearly established from that. (64)

Once it is established that substitutes (ādeśas) possess denotative power, the word-sphoṭa (padasphoṭa) is likewise established; thus he says, "Now," and so forth. "Substitutes" refers to *tiṅ*, visarga, and the like. The underlying idea is this: when it is established that phonemes uttered in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*) possess denotative power, the denotative capacity of the word—which consists of such a collocation of phonemes—is also established. This is because the recollection of meaning for each individual phoneme contradicts experience; furthermore, if each phoneme were individually meaningful, they would incur the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), which would lead to the undesired elision of the *n* in words such as *dhanam* and *vanam* by rules such as "the *n* at the end of a nominal stem is not elided."

Furthermore, this expressive power (*vācakatva-śakti*) resides in the final letter alone, because there is no evidence for the power to reside distributively across multiple letters. The impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding letter act as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) in the production of the cognition of the meaning by the final letter; thus, the cognition of the meaning does not arise from the utterance of that [final letter] alone. This was stated in order to refute another view held by the proponents of the *varṇasphoṭa* (the theory that the phonemes themselves are the sphoṭa).

For if one were to say "Rāma exists" (*rāmo 'sti*), and instead of saying "rāma," one were to utter the vowel *o* one *ghaṭikā* later, it would follow that the meaning is understood; therefore, the specific sequence (*ānupūrvī*) itself must be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the expressive power. This is the general direction [of the argument]. || 64 ||
The Definition of the Undivided Word-Sphoṭa (the definition of the conventional word-sphoṭa as "a word is that which ends in a nominal or verbal suffix"):

He states the view of those who accept the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of the conventionally defined word—"a word is that which ends in a nominal or verbal suffix" (*suptiṅantaṃ padam*)—as follows:
"In [words] such as *ghaṭena*, no distinction between base (*prakṛti*) and so forth exists."
For even here, as in the case of the loss of wealth and so forth, confusion is indeed observed. || 65 ||

In examples such as *ghaṭena*, the analysis into "ghaṭe" as the base (*prakṛti*) and "na" as the suffix (*pratyaya*), or "ghaṭ" as the base and "ena" as the suffix, is impossible because, under the principle that "all [words] are substitutes for all words," it is impossible to specifically identify the base and the suffix; thus, they do not possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). Since the grammarians' analysis is easily understood, he states by way of an illustration: "In cases such as *vas* and *nas*"—the meaning is that since the rule "for the plural, *vas* and *nas*" prescribes these as substitutes for the entire group [of case-endings], no such division [into base and suffix] is possible here. || 65 ||

The determination of the sentence-sphoṭa consisting of a collection of nominal and verbal suffixes (the determination of the sentence-sphoṭa as a collection of words ending in nominal and verbal suffixes):
He states this even regarding the sentence in the form of a collection of nominal and verbal suffixes—
having seen "hare'va" and so forth, determine the sentence-sphoṭa.
If it is argued that the specific relation [of a word] to its meaning is not apprehended, this is equally true in the case of a word.

If [it is argued] that based on the grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*), that [denotative power] exists now in the word-form (*pada*), let it be so also in the case of the meaning. In examples such as *hare'va* and *viṣṇo'va*, when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) according to the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* has occurred, the division between those two words is not easily discernible. Thus, even when the individual words are unknown, because verbal cognition arises from the knowledge of the power residing in the whole (*samudāyaśakti*), the power must necessarily reside in the whole as well. And in this way, even though the base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) are not specifically known, since cognition arises through the conventional derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the whole, the power must necessarily reside there too—this is the intended meaning.

In reality, just as the cognition of word-meanings arises from words, so too does the cognition of sentence-meaning arise from a sentence; therefore, just as there is a power of word-meanings residing in words, one must admit a power of sentence-meaning residing in the sentence. Thus, the *padasphoṭa* (word-atom) and *vākyasphoṭa* (sentence-atom) are established. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even someone lacking such linguistic proficiency would have cognition upon hearing "jar," "objectness," "bringing," and "effort" [separately]. Furthermore, even when the word-meanings are presented as they are in the case of "bring the jar," there is no cognition if there is no knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

If it is argued that, in the cognition "the bringing of the jar" (*ghaṭakarmakam ānayanam*), the cause is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the nominal stem denoting the jar, followed by the case-ending expressing the objecthood (*karmatva*), followed by the verbal root, and followed by the finite verb; and that for one who possesses knowledge of this causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), such knowledge is also a cause [of the sentence-meaning], then the *vākya-sphoṭa* (sentence-sphoṭa) is established. This is because, just as there is a causal relation between the knowledge of the word-potency (*padaśakti*)—which consists in being a signifier—and the cognition of the meaning of words like "jar," so too must there be a causal relation with respect to the cognition of the specific sentence-meaning.

This is because it is postulated that the knowledge of the sentence-potency (*vākya-śakti*)—which consists in the denotative power residing in a sentence in the form of the co-utterance of words—is also a cause [of verbal cognition]; for potency (*śakti*) is precisely the causality of the knowledge of a word's function (*vṛtti*) as the object of the knowledge that presents the meaning. And this is logical, since, by parsimony (*lāghava*), the knowledge of the function is established as the cause of all verbal cognitions (*śābdabodha*) simply through the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*). This has been analyzed in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. Thus is the proof of sentence-potency.

One might object: "Since the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is something previously unknown (*apūrva*), how can there be a grasp of its expressive power (*śaktigraha*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the meaning"—the word "of the sentence" is to be supplied as the remainder. If it is argued that the specific expressive power of a sentence with respect to its sentence-meaning cannot be grasped, then the same applies to the word (*pada*). Even in the view that the expressive power resides only in the word regarding the aspect of syntactic relation (*anvaya*), the impossibility of grasping that [power] is equal; such is the meaning.

The sense is this: if the "crippled power" (kubja-śakti) theory holds that the word's power is known with respect to the individual word-meanings while it remains unknown with respect to the relation (anvaya), then my own position—that the power of the sentence is useful precisely when it is unknown—is equally accepted as a doctrine. Now, one might object: "For one who observes the linguistic usage of elders, the apprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs through the mind just as it does for the word-meanings. To this he replies, "Because of inference" (lakṣaṇāt): that by which something is characterized or inferred is an "inference" (lakṣaṇa); [it refers to] the mind (manas). Thus, the apprehension of the sentence-meaning is likewise achieved through the mind.

The phrase "even in the word" (*api-padam*) should be understood as following the words "word" and "subsequent. If it is argued that [the meaning] is not grasped even in the word because of its secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), then let it be so in the sentence as well—this is the remainder of the sense. In reality, however, the grasping of that [meaning] occurs first for the sentence as a whole in its collective sense; it should be understood that subsequently, through the method of addition and subtraction (*āpāyopāya*), the grasping of each individual [word-meaning] occurs. || 66 ||
Regarding the capacity of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*), there is the consensus of the Mīmāṃsakas and others;
he states that this alone is the position of the Mīmāṃsakas and certain followers of Vedānta:
"For those who know that in every case the meaning of a sentence is indeed indicated (*lakṣya*) alone..."
Those followers of Bhaṭṭa also speak in this very way regarding the application of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

The term "Bhāṭṭas" is an elliptical designation for their followers, such as Vācaspati, Kalpataru, and others. Now, it may be argued that both of the aforementioned positions are untenable; for since production and manifestation cannot occur simultaneously, there can be no cognition of a word in the form of a collection of phonemes that are both produced and manifested at once.

If it is argued that, in that case, the cognition of a sentence—which is by nature an aggregate of those [phonemes]—is even more impossible, we say no. At the time of the perception of a subsequent phoneme, the presence of preceding phonemes related to it by the relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*) is easily grasped; likewise, at the time of perceiving the one following that, the presence of that specific phoneme as qualified by its predecessors is easily grasped. Thus, just as the status of being a *pada* (word) consisting of such a sequence is easily grasped, so too is the status of being a *vākya* (sentence). || 67 ||
Now, regarding the exposition of the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa, he states the position of indivisibility:
"In a word, phonemes do not exist; nor do parts exist within phonemes."
There is no absolute separation whatsoever between words and the sentence.

In cases such as *pade pacati*, it is not the individual phonemes [that constitute the word]; therefore, the remainder of the argument is that a word is not a collection of phonemes. He states this by way of an illustration: "In the case of the phonemes"—meaning that just as the phonemes *e*, *o*, *ṛ*, and so forth, do not have constituent parts even though they are perceived as such; in some places, the reading is simply *iva* (as if). Likewise, he speaks regarding the sentence: "From the sentence"—the meaning is that there is no distinction or difference between words and the sentence.

The meaning is this: both the sentence and the word are indeed indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*), and not a mere collection of phonemes (*varṇa*), because there is no evidence for the postulation of an infinite number of phonemes. This is because the distinctness of cognitions such as "the letter *ka*" and "the letter *ga*" is possible by taking into account a specific generic difference (*vaijātya*) residing in the conjunctions of air—which are intended to produce those respective phonemes—and which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for either the capacity to generate or the capacity to manifest those respective phonemes. For it is clearly stated in the *Bhāmatī* on the *Devatādhikaraṇa*: "Properties such as high pitch, which reside in the air, are superimposed upon the phonemes."

Nor should it be argued that in this case, the conjunction with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*) itself might be the signifier (*vācaka*); for it is established by experience that only the *ka*-sounds and other phonemes, which are perceived through direct perception, possess the status of being signifiers. Thus, because the status of being a signifier cannot otherwise be accounted for, and because of the cognitions "this is that very word," "this is that very sentence," and "this is that very *ga*-sound," the indivisible *sphoṭa* is established. By this, the view that the phonemes themselves are the signifiers—on the grounds that no *sphoṭa* is experienced apart from the *ga*, *au*, and visarga in words such as *gaur*—is refuted; for those [phonemes] are not distinct from the *sphoṭa*.
Refutation of Kaiyaṭa:

As for the argument that if phonemes were individually expressive, there would be the contingency of understanding the meaning from each one; whereas, as for a collection, it is simply impossible to have a cognition of those [phonemes] which possess a sequence, whether they are produced very rapidly or manifested in that same way.

However, Kaiyaṭa maintains that the simultaneous occurrence of a single cognition comprising the entire sequence—made possible by the cooperation of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from the experience of each preceding letter—is common to cases such as *sara-rosa*, *rāja-jarā*, and *nadī-dīnā*, and thus results in an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, he asserts that the *sphoṭa* alone, being impartite and manifested by sound (*nāda*), is the signifier. This is untenable, because the possibility of the cognition of the word has already been established. Furthermore, this view is subject to the dilemma of whether individual letters or the letters combined together act as the manifestors. [This concludes] the defense of our own position.

If it is argued: "But this same fault applies even to your own position, because the dilemma remains as to whether the air-conjunctions intended to produce each respective letter (*varṇa*) are manifesters individually or collectively," we reply: The conjunctions are indeed manifesters individually; however, they function in various ways—some as the quality of *ga*, some as the quality of *au*, and some as the quality of *visarga*. For this very reason, the non-acceptance of the letters as being distinct from those [conjunctions] is also logically justified.

In this way, the property of being preceded by *gha* is grasped in the letter *ṭ* through the relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*). There is no dispute regarding such word-cognition being the cause [of the understanding of meaning]. However, "immediate succession" must be defined as being the object of a cognition that arises in a moment whose locus is the locus of one's own cognition. For this very reason, the usage of the elder Naiyāyikas—such as the definition of "word-order" (*ānupūrvī*) as being the object of the cognition of *ṭ* immediately following the cognition of *gha*—is established. And thus, there is no fault whatsoever. [This concludes] the refutation of the *Parimala*.

By this [it is asked]: in the case of synonyms, is there one single *sphoṭa* or many? Not the first, because for one who has grasped the expressive power (*śakti*) in the word "ghaṭa" alone, there would follow the cognition of "kalaśa" and other synonyms. Nor can it be argued that the grasp of power regarding the manifestation of a particular synonym is the cause of the cognition of the meaning upon hearing that synonym; for if that were so, since the grasp of power must necessarily occur for every individual synonym, it would be more appropriate that the cause is the grasp of power residing in each respective synonym. This being the case, simplicity (*lāghava*) dictates that the cause is simply the state of having grasped the power (*śaktigrahatvena*).

Otherwise, [the opponent's view] is refuted by the *Parimala*, which states that if it were the case [that the word-meaning relation resides in synonyms], there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) because one would have to grasp the expressive power residing in what is manifested through those synonyms. Nor is the second alternative [correct], because, compared to postulating a power for those infinite words, it is simpler to postulate the power in the already established phonemes (*varṇa*). This is because the acceptance of multiple powers in synonyms is universally established, and because the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) that delimits them has been demonstrated previously.
Such is the view of Dīkṣita in the *Śabdakaustubha*.

In the *Śabdakaustubha*, however, it is established that the sphoṭa is indeed distinct from the phonemes, because there is the cognition "this is a word" regarding a series of phonemes; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that things such as a jar could not be established as distinct from their constituent potsherds. || 68 ||

Regarding the defense of the authority of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) under the theory of the indivisible word (*akhaṇḍasphoṭa*): one might object that, in this case, the treatise would result in being non-authoritative, because the word is indivisible, whereas the purpose of the treatise is merely to derive words through bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). To resolve this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, this conceptual construction is resorted to, just as in the case of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so forth."
The means for attaining the goal are not fixed, as they exist for the purpose of realizing that goal. || 69 ||

The syntactical connection extends up to the words "for the purpose of attaining the goal. This is the intended meaning: just as in the Bhṛguvallī, where Bhṛgu Vāruṇi asked Varuṇa about Brahman, and he replied, "Food"; and after [Bhṛgu] had understood its origin and so forth, he asked again, whereupon Brahman was taught as that which is to be known as "the tail, the support of Brahman," following the five sheaths consisting of food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss. In that context, the exposition of the five sheaths is for the sake of awakening one to the pure Brahman.

Just as the exposition of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) in the *Ānandavallī* is for the purpose of awakening one to the real, pure Brahman, so too the exposition of stems (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth, is solely for the purpose of awakening one to the real *sphoṭa*.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the *sphoṭa*, which is directly perceptible, can be understood even through hearing and other means, grammar is not the means to that end. To this he says: "The means [are many]," because one means does not invalidate another means. Thus, a specific generic quality (*vaijātya*) is postulated in the knowledge produced by the study of grammar, just as there is a specific quality in the recollection of meaning produced by a mantra.

Just as [the study of grammar] serves the knowledge of Brahman produced by Vedānta, so too that knowledge has its utility for the purification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) through sacrifices and other rites, as well as for the purification of the body and so forth; and it serves as the cause of heaven, liberation, and the like, either directly or indirectly.
As it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"It is the gateway to liberation and the remedy for the impurities of speech."
The purifier of all sciences shines as the supreme science.
This is the first station for those ascending the steps of spiritual perfection;
this is that straight royal road for those seeking liberation.
"In this case, one who has transcended error perceives only the [ultimate reality].

Nor can there be a cognition of the real *sphoṭa* through an unreal conceptualization of stems and suffixes, because it will be shown later that its unreality is unestablished. In this way, the "analogy of the line-drawn gavaya" and so forth are included by the word "etcetera. || 69 ||

But surely, since both the sphoṭa and the universals (jāti) of the phonemes are eternal, it would not be possible for there to be such an expression as "the letter *ka* has arisen. Furthermore, if the universal residing in the conjunctions of air were to manifest in the sphoṭa, it would follow that cognitions of *ka*, etc., are erroneous. To this, he says:
"For even others accept that imagined [entities] serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Indeed, others consider even accents, length, and so forth to belong to something other than the phonemes themselves. (70)

He states the grounds for accepting [the permanence of phonemes] with the words "svaradairghyādyapi" ("even accent, length, and so forth"). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), production and destruction are included. Properties such as being acute (*udātta*) do not reside in the phoneme (*varṇa*), because that [phoneme] is unitary and eternal. And this [unity and eternity] is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same [phoneme]. Nor is the object of that recognition the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the universal *gatva* (phonemic-ness). For it is impossible to abandon the non-difference of the individual instances (*vyakti*)—which also appears [in cognition]—without a subverting proof (*bādhaka*).

Nor does the perception of production (utpatti) constitute a sublation [of the permanence of phonemes], because production—defined as existence following prior non-existence—is contrary to experience regarding phonemes. For this very reason, there is the cognition and linguistic usage "he utters a phoneme," and not the cognition or usage "he produces a phoneme. Furthermore, "being uttered" consists in being characterized by a manifestation produced by the contact of the palate, lips, and so forth. Moreover, since the production and other properties residing in the manifesting sound (dhvani) can be attributed to the phoneme through a causal chain, that [perception of production] does not prove the existence of a distinct phoneme.

Furthermore, because it is accepted that [the cognition] is ultimately based on the phonemes (*varṇa*), it is not an error. It is specified that the error lies only in the aspect of the direct relation [between the word and its meaning].

Even that is equal to your own admission of error regarding the non-difference of individuals in the case of the judgment "this is that" (*so 'yam*). However, for me, there is no postulation of additional phonemes, their prior absences, or their destructions; thus, my position possesses the advantage of parsimony (*lāghava*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the existence of sound (*dhvani*) at the place where a phoneme (*varṇa*) occurs, nor that its occurrence is impossible due to the absence of conch-shells or other such sources that produce it; for it is observed that when the tongue slightly falls away from its respective articulatory point during the utterance of the letter *ka* and others, while the phoneme is not produced, sound is produced. This is because one must postulate that the impact of the tongue and the contact between the air and the throat are the generators of sound.

Furthermore, since that [property] exists even at the place where the letter is produced, the postulation of a relationship of counteracting and counteracted (pratibandhya-pratibandhaka-bhāva) would be without proof for you alone; thus, there is a "reversal of the burden" (viparīta-gaurava). Likewise, due to mutual contradiction, it is not logical for properties such as acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), short (hrasva), and long (dīrgha) to reside in the letter itself—this is their intention. And so, the resolution of the cognitions of production and so forth, as well as the establishment of their validity, is equally [difficult] for the opponent as well; therefore, the sense is that the answer is by means of a "counter-objection" (pratibandi) itself. || 70 ||
Thus, there are five types of individual *sphoṭas*.
Now, the description of the class-*sphoṭa* (*jātisphoṭa*) is given: he states the class-*sphoṭa*—
Just as in the case of capability, let the parsimony of the universal (jāti) be observed in its capacity;
or let there be a distinction among the phonemes based on adventitious conditions (aupādhika), like the high and low pitches [of a sound]. (71)

The point is this: phonemes (*varṇa*) are, first of all, indispensable. And according to the reasoning stated, just as one might say "this is that *ga*-sound," one could also say "this *ha*-sound which is heard is that same *ga*-sound," because the *sphoṭa* is a single entity; furthermore, the cognition "this is a *ga*-sound, not a *ha*-sound" would not arise [if there were no distinct phonemes]. Moreover, must "ga-ness" (*gatva*) and so forth be admitted in the *sphoṭa*, or not? In the first case, let that very thing be the *ga*-sound itself, since those who maintain the eternity of phonemes do not accept a separate "ga-ness. Thus, the postulation of a separate *sphoṭa* is merely a superfluous assumption (*gauṇatvam*).

In the final view, there is a contradiction with the cognition of the letter *ga* and so forth. If it is argued that such a cognition occurs by superimposing a specific generic quality (*vaijātya*) residing in the conjunction with air or residing in the sound (*dhvani*), we say no; for a cognition cannot be considered erroneous without a subverting factor (*bādhaka*). Or, let the conjunction with air itself be the letter *ga*; if it is objected that its being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*) is a defect, we reply that this is justifiable as in the case of [imperceptible] qualities (*dharma*), so there is no need for the theory of *sphoṭa*. Therefore, letters certainly exist, but they are not the denoters (*vācaka*). This is because of the principle of complexity (*gaurava*), and because, according to the logic of the section on "Form" (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*), just as the universal (*jāti*) alone is rightly held to be the denoted, it is likewise logical that it alone is the denoter.

Because the cognition "this is the word *hari*" arises through a subsequent mental apprehension, the knowledge of the word *hari* functions as the cause with respect to the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the object *hari*; and since a specific universal (*jāti*) must necessarily be postulated as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that [causal relation], it follows that this universal is required. Nor can the sequential order of the phonemes alone suffice to account for these two delimitations, for otherwise even a jar or the universal "jar-ness" would be rendered superfluous by the specific conjunctions and the shape of the clay, etc., which could serve as their grounds.

Therefore, that *jāti* (universal) alone is the expressive [element], and it is the delimiting factor by virtue of identity (*tādātmya*). Now, an objection is raised: "In cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, since those two *jātis* exist [in both words], there would be no difference in the comprehension of meaning. To this, he says: "Or, [it is] conditional (*aupādhikaḥ*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). The condition (*upādhi*) is the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*), and that alone is the manifester of the specific *jāti*; thus, the difference pertains to the cognition which serves as the instrument, and so there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is the intended meaning. He provides an illustration regarding the distinction in cognition caused by the condition: "of the phonemes," etc. (Kārikā 71).

Now, since the universal (jāti) exists in each individual phoneme (varṇa), it might follow that the meaning would be understood from each one individually; therefore, he says: "The universal, manifested by multiple individuals, is known as *sphoṭa*. By some, these very individuals are conceived as being the sounds (*dhvani*). (72)

The universal (*jāti*) itself, manifested by numerous individual phonetic manifestations (*varṇavyakti*), is known as *sphoṭa*; that is to say, it is the means of cognition (*bodhikā*) by virtue of its etymological sense (*yogārthatayā*). By this, the objection that because *sphoṭa* is eternal, there would be the consequence of constant cognition of meaning at all times, is refuted. This is the intended meaning: although the aforementioned defect exists in the view of *varṇasphoṭa*, it does not exist in the views of *padasphoṭa* and *vākyasphoṭa*, because in those cases, its occurrence as a collective property (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*) is established by the very cognition of the substratum (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). The remaining point is that some maintain that the individual manifestations (*vyaktayaḥ*) are indeed sounds (*dhvanayaḥ*), since there is no difference between sound and phoneme (*dhvani-varṇa*).

For it is said in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "The learned grammarians have employed the term 'dhvani' for that word which manifests the manifested form of *sphoṭa*, which constitutes the primary element. (72)
Regarding the definition of "universal" (jāti): Now, what is that universal? To this he says:
"In every entity, there exist two parts, one real and one unreal."
That which is real there is the genus (jāti); the individuals (vyakti) are considered unreal. || 73 ||

"For every individual entity"—that is, for each object. The universal (*jāti*) is the real aspect; the individuals are unreal. The meaning is that the universal is indeed Brahman itself as qualified by this or that particular manifestation. And it has been stated by Kaiyaṭa: "The meaning is that the reality of Brahman, delimited by unreal adjuncts (*upādhi*), is what is denoted by the word 'substance' (*dravya*). And: "The very reality of Brahman appears in the form of the word."

How, then, is Kaiyaṭa’s position consistent with the statement that even the universal (jāti) such as "cowness" is impermanent because it does not exist in the vision of Brahman, according to the Vedic declaration, "All this is indeed the Self"? It should be understood that he adopts an alternative view, namely, that [the cause of non-existence] is either ignorance (avidyā) or a specific property arising from ignorance (āvidyaka). || 73 ||

He clarifies that very point regarding the element of truth: "The essence of sound, when thus extracted as stainless, is said to be Brahman itself, the Imperishable; salutation to that Perfect Self. (74)

The meaning is as follows: There is a twofold creation established by the Śruti, namely, "I shall manifest name and form. In that regard, the reality of name is the very same as that of form; the portion consisting of the grammatical derivation (prakriyā) is merely the manifestation of ignorance (avidyā). And it has been said in the Vākyapadīya:
"In the scriptures, it is ignorance itself that is described through various distinctions of grammatical derivation."
The undertaking of all things is beginningless, yet Brahman is eternal. Thus [it is said].

By the phrase "Brahman alone," he indicates that [the Self] possesses the quality of illuminating both itself and others, as established by such scriptural passages as: "In this state, this person is self-luminous," "Everything shines after Him alone as He shines," and "By His light all this is illumined. Furthermore, he indicates that it is denoted by the etymological term *sphoṭa*, meaning "that from which the meaning bursts forth clearly. Finally, for the sake of unimpeded progress, he utters an auspicious benediction in the form of praise and salutation with the words beginning "To the Perfect Self," and so on. (74)
I adorn with the illustrious *Bhūṣaṇasāra* my preceptor, the Lord of All, who bestows all fruits without exception and who is adorned by Śeṣa. || 1 ||
The auspicious *kārikās* composed by the eminent Bhaṭṭojī Dīkṣita have been explained in great detail by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa. (2)

Thus ends the *Sphoṭavāda* in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, the son of Raṅgojibhaṭṭa, who was preeminent among those who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the illustrious *Pada*, *Vākya*, and *Pramāṇa* sciences.
This work is also completed.
